Appendix A Model Setup

A.1 Model Architecture

We consider a single-layer transformer network with a single linear attention head. The attention mechanism employed is purely linear, omitting the softmax normalization typically found in standard attention mechanisms.

A.2 Variables

We define the key variables used in our model as follows:

  • •

    Input Data Pairs: We are given NN pairs of dd-dimensional data points (xi,yi)∈ℝd×ℝd(x_{i},y_{i})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d} for i=1,…,Ni=1,\dots,N, and a query point xq∈ℝdx_{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

  • •

    Embedding Dimension: The embedding dimension is set to D=2​dD=2d.

  • •

    Input Sequence Matrix: For an input sequence of NN data pairs and a query point (x1,y1,…,xN,yn,xq)(x_{1},y_{1},\dots,x_{N},y_{n},x_{q}), the input to the transformer is constructed as a matrix Z∈ℝD×(N+1)Z\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times(N+1)}. Specifically, ZZ is defined as:

    Z=[x1x2…xNxqy1y2…yN𝟎d]∈ℝD×(N+1),Z=\begin{bmatrix}x_{1}&x_{2}&\dots&x_{N}&x_{q}\\ y_{1}&y_{2}&\dots&y_{N}&\mathbf{0}_{d}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times(N+1)}, (A1)

    where 𝟎d∈ℝd\mathbf{0}_{d}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is a zero vector of dimension dd.

  • •

    Weight Matrices:

    • –

      Combined Query-Key Weight Matrix: WQ∈ℝD×DW^{Q}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times D}. We define a submatrix q∈ℝD×dq\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times d} comprising the first dd columns of WQW^{Q}. This submatrix is further partitioned as q=(q1q2)q=\begin{pmatrix}q_{1}\\ q_{2}\end{pmatrix}, where q1,q2∈ℝd×dq_{1},q_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}.

    • –

      Output Projection Weight Matrix: WP∈ℝD×DW^{P}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times D}. We define a submatrix pT∈ℝd×Dp^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times D} comprising the bottom dd rows of WPW^{P}. This submatrix is further partitioned as pT=(p1p2)p^{T}=\begin{pmatrix}p_{1}&p_{2}\end{pmatrix}, where p1,p2∈ℝd×dp_{1},p_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}.

A.3 Linear Transformer

The output of the linear attention head, before the residual connection, is given by:

O=WP​(Z​Z⊤N)​WQ​Z∈ℝD×(N+1),O=W^{P}\left(\frac{ZZ^{\top}}{N}\right)W^{Q}Z\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times(N+1)}, (A2)

where the attention operation is normalized by NN.

The output of the single-layer linear transformer network, denoted as f⁡(Z)∈ℝD×(N+1)f(Z)\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times(N+1)}, is obtained by adding a residual connection:

f⁡(Z)=Z+O=Z+WP​(Z​Z⊤N)​WQ​Z∈ℝD×(N+1).f(Z)=Z+O=Z+W^{P}\left(\frac{ZZ^{\top}}{N}\right)W^{Q}Z\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times(N+1)}. (A3)

A.4 Predictor

We are interested in the model’s prediction for the query input xqx_{q}. This prediction is derived from the (N+1)(N+1)-th column of the transformer network’s output, f⁡(Z)f(Z). Specifically, the prediction y^∈ℝd\hat{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is obtained from the bottom dd elements of the (N+1)(N+1)-th column of f⁡(Z)f(Z).

Due to the specific embedding structure defined in Section A.2 and the output reading mechanism, the prediction can be simplified to:

y^=(p⊤​Γ^​q)​xq∈ℝd,\hat{y}=\left(p^{\top}\hat{\Gamma}q\right)x_{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, (A4)

where Γ^=Z​Z⊤N∈ℝD×D\hat{\Gamma}=\frac{ZZ^{\top}}{N}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times D} is the empirical covariance matrix of the input ZZ. Note that the matrix product (p⊤​Γ^​q)(p^{\top}\hat{\Gamma}q) results in a d×dd\times d matrix. The explicit derivation of this simplification is provided in Section A.9.

A.5 Loss Function

To train the model, we employ the mean squared error (MSE) loss function, defined as:

ℒ=12​‖y^−yq‖22=12​‖(p⊤​Γ^​q)​xq−yq‖22.\mathcal{L}=\frac{1}{2}\|\hat{y}-y_{q}\|_{2}^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\left\|\left(p^{\top}\hat{\Gamma}q\right)x_{q}-y_{q}\right\|_{2}^{2}. (A5)

This loss function quantifies the discrepancy between the model’s prediction y^\hat{y} and the ground truth yqy_{q}.

A.6 Goal

The primary objective is to mathematically analyze this exactly solvable model of a linear transformer for in-context regression. Specifically, we aim to understand the learning dynamics and mechanisms through which the model predicts yqy_{q} based on the provided in-context examples {(xi,yi)}i=1N\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}.

A.7 Key Assumptions

Our analysis relies on the following key assumptions regarding the model architecture and setup:

  • •

    Single-layer, single-head linear transformer. We consider a simplified transformer architecture with only one layer and a single attention head, both of which are linear.

  • •

    No softmax in attention mechanism. The linear attention mechanism omits the softmax normalization, resulting in a purely linear operation.

  • •

    Specific embedding mechanism without positional tokens. We employ a specific input embedding structure as defined in Section A.2, without the use of positional tokens.

  • •

    Prediction focused on the (N+𝟏)(\boldsymbol{N+1})-th output token. We focus our analysis on the prediction derived from the (N+1)(N+1)-th output token, corresponding to the query input xqx_{q}.

A.8 Task Setup

We aim to train the linear transformer to perform in-context linear regression. To this end, we generate training data by sampling random instances of linear regression problems.

A.8.1 x-data Generation

During training, the input data xx is sampled from a multivariate Gaussian distribution with zero mean and a diagonal covariance matrix Σx∈ℝd×d\Sigma_{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}. Formally,

x∼𝒩⁡(𝟎d,Σx).x\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{0}_{d},\Sigma_{x}\right). (A6)

Here, 𝟎d∈ℝd\mathbf{0}_{d}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is a zero-mean vector, and Σx=diag​(σx,12,…,σx,d2)\Sigma_{x}=\text{diag}(\sigma_{x,1}^{2},\dots,\sigma_{x,d}^{2}) is a diagonal covariance matrix, where σx,i2>0\sigma_{x,i}^{2}>0 are the variances along each dimension.

A.8.2 Transformation Matrix WW Generation

The transformation matrix W∈ℝd×dW\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} is generated to define the linear regression task. First, we sample dd eigenvalues λ1,…,λd\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{d} from a standard multivariate Gaussian distribution 𝒩⁡(𝟎d,Id)\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}_{d},I_{d}). We then construct a diagonal matrix Λ=diag​(λ1,…,λd)∈ℝd×d\Lambda=\text{diag}(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{d})\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}. For a fixed orthogonal matrix V∈ℝd×dV\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}, the transformation matrix WW is defined as:

W=V​Λ​V⊤∈ℝd×d.W=V\Lambda V^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}. (A7)

Note that, due to the zero mean of the eigenvalues, the expected value of WW is 𝔼⁡[W]=0\mathbb{E}[W]=0. Furthermore, 𝔼⁡[W​W⊤]=V​𝔼​[Λ2]​V⊤=V​Id​V⊤=V​V⊤\mathbb{E}[WW^{\top}]=V\mathbb{E}[\Lambda^{2}]V^{\top}=VI_{d}V^{\top}=VV^{\top}, since 𝔼⁡[Λ2]=Id\mathbb{E}[\Lambda^{2}]=I_{d} when eigenvalues are sampled from standard Gaussian. We consider PP independent regression tasks, each defined by a transformation matrix WμW^{\mu} for μ=1,…,P\mu=1,\dots,P. These matrices {Wμ}μ=1P\{W^{\mu}\}_{\mu=1}^{P} are sampled at the beginning of training and remain fixed throughout the training process.

A.8.3 y-data Generation and Empirical Covariance

For each regression task μ\mu defined by WμW^{\mu}, we generate the corresponding yy-data. First, we sample x1,…,xN,xq∈ℝdx_{1},\dots,x_{N},x_{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} from the distribution defined in Section A.8.1. Then, for each xix_{i} (i=1,…,Ni=1,\dots,N), we generate yiy_{i} using the linear transformation yi=Wμ​xiy_{i}=W^{\mu}x_{i}. For the query point xqx_{q}, the ground truth yqy_{q} is similarly given by yq=Wμ​xqy_{q}=W^{\mu}x_{q}.

For a specific task μ\mu, the input sequence matrix ZμZ^{\mu} is constructed as:

Zμ=[x1x2…xNxqWμ​x1Wμ​x2…Wμ​xN𝟎d]∈ℝD×(N+1).Z^{\mu}=\begin{bmatrix}x_{1}&x_{2}&\dots&x_{N}&x_{q}\\ W^{\mu}x_{1}&W^{\mu}x_{2}&\dots&W^{\mu}x_{N}&\mathbf{0}_{d}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times(N+1)}. (A8)

The model’s prediction is based on the empirical covariance matrix of ZμZ^{\mu}, denoted as Γ^μ=1N​Zμ​(Zμ)⊤∈ℝD×D\hat{\Gamma}^{\mu}=\frac{1}{N}Z^{\mu}(Z^{\mu})^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times D}. To derive an explicit form for Γ^μ\hat{\Gamma}^{\mu}, we first compute Zμ​(Zμ)⊤Z^{\mu}(Z^{\mu})^{\top}:

Zμ​(Zμ)⊤\displaystyle Z^{\mu}(Z^{\mu})^{\top} =[x1…xNxqWμ​x1…Wμ​xN𝟎d]​[x1⊤(Wμ​x1)⊤xN⊤(Wμ​xN)⊤xq⊤𝟎d⊤]\displaystyle=\begin{bmatrix}x_{1}&\dots&x_{N}&x_{q}\\ W^{\mu}x_{1}&\dots&W^{\mu}x_{N}&\mathbf{0}_{d}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x_{1}^{\top}&(W^{\mu}x_{1})^{\top}\\ \vdots&\vdots\\ x_{N}^{\top}&(W^{\mu}x_{N})^{\top}\\ x_{q}^{\top}&\mathbf{0}_{d}^{\top}\end{bmatrix}
=[∑i=1Nxi​xi⊤+xq​xq⊤∑i=1Nxi​(Wμ​xi)⊤∑i=1NWμ​xi​xi⊤∑i=1NWμ​xi​(Wμ​xi)⊤]\displaystyle=\begin{bmatrix}\sum_{i=1}^{N}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}+x_{q}x_{q}^{\top}&\sum_{i=1}^{N}x_{i}(W^{\mu}x_{i})^{\top}\\ \sum_{i=1}^{N}W^{\mu}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}&\sum_{i=1}^{N}W^{\mu}x_{i}(W^{\mu}x_{i})^{\top}\end{bmatrix}
=[∑i=1Nxi​xi⊤+xq​xq⊤∑i=1Nxi​xi⊤​(Wμ)⊤∑i=1NWμ​xi​xi⊤∑i=1NWμ​xi​xi⊤​(Wμ)⊤].\displaystyle=\begin{bmatrix}\sum_{i=1}^{N}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}+x_{q}x_{q}^{\top}&\sum_{i=1}^{N}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}(W^{\mu})^{\top}\\ \sum_{i=1}^{N}W^{\mu}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}&\sum_{i=1}^{N}W^{\mu}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}(W^{\mu})^{\top}\end{bmatrix}.

Thus, the empirical covariance matrix Γ^μ\hat{\Gamma}^{\mu} is given by:

Γ^μ=1N​Zμ​(Zμ)⊤=[1N​∑i=1Nxi​xi⊤+1N​xq​xq⊤1N​∑i=1Nxi​xi⊤​(Wμ)⊤1N​∑i=1NWμ​xi​xi⊤1N​∑i=1NWμ​xi​xi⊤​(Wμ)⊤]∈ℝD×D.\hat{\Gamma}^{\mu}=\frac{1}{N}Z^{\mu}(Z^{\mu})^{\top}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}+\frac{1}{N}x_{q}x_{q}^{\top}&\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}(W^{\mu})^{\top}\\ \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}W^{\mu}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}&\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}W^{\mu}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}(W^{\mu})^{\top}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times D}. (A9)

Let Σ^x=1N​∑i=1Nxi​xi⊤\hat{\Sigma}_{x}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top} denote the empirical covariance of the training xx-data {xi}i=1N\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}. Then, Γ^μ\hat{\Gamma}^{\mu} can be expressed in block form as:

Γ^μ=[Σ^x+1N​xq​xq⊤Σ^x​(Wμ)⊤Wμ​Σ^xWμ​Σ^x​(Wμ)⊤].\hat{\Gamma}^{\mu}=\begin{bmatrix}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}+\frac{1}{N}x_{q}x_{q}^{\top}&\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top}\\ W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}&W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top}\end{bmatrix}. (A10)

In some subsequent derivations, for simplicity of notation, we might approximate Γ^μ\hat{\Gamma}^{\mu} by ignoring the term 1N​xq​xq⊤\frac{1}{N}x_{q}x_{q}^{\top} in the top-left block, leading to:

Γ^μ≈[Σ^xΣ^x​(Wμ)⊤Wμ​Σ^xWμ​Σ^x​(Wμ)⊤].\hat{\Gamma}^{\mu}\approx\begin{bmatrix}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}&\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top}\\ W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}&W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top}\end{bmatrix}. (A11)

This approximation is valid when NN is sufficiently large such that the contribution of the query point xqx_{q} to the empirical covariance is negligible compared to the contribution of the in-context examples {xi}i=1N\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}.

A.8.4 Training Setup

We train the model using stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with a learning rate λ\lambda. Training proceeds in task-centric epochs. In each epoch, we iterate through the set of PP regression tasks {Wμ}μ=1P\{W^{\mu}\}_{\mu=1}^{P}. For each task WμW^{\mu}, we sample a batch of in-context examples {(xi,yi)}i=1N\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N} and a query point xqx_{q}, and compute the loss function ℒμ\mathcal{L}^{\mu} as defined in Section A.5. We then update the model parameters using the gradient of ℒμ\mathcal{L}^{\mu} with respect to the parameters, accumulated over the batch. A training epoch is completed once all PP tasks have been presented to the model. Using batches for gradient updates helps to reduce noise in the training process.

A.9 Simplified Predictor

In this section, we derive the simplified form of the predictor given in Equation (A4). Recall from Equation (A3) that the output of the linear transformer is given by:

f⁡(Z)=Z+WP​(Z​Z⊤N)​WQ​Z=Z+WP​Γ^​WQ​Z.f(Z)=Z+W^{P}\left(\frac{ZZ^{\top}}{N}\right)W^{Q}Z=Z+W^{P}\hat{\Gamma}W^{Q}Z. (A12)

We are interested in the prediction y^\hat{y}, which is obtained from the bottom dd elements of the (N+1)(N+1)-th column of f⁡(Z)f(Z).

First, let’s consider the (N+1)(N+1)-th column of the input matrix ZZ, which is given by (xq𝟎d)∈ℝD\begin{pmatrix}x_{q}\\ \mathbf{0}_{d}\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{D}. Then, the (N+1)(N+1)-th column of the matrix product WQ​ZW^{Q}Z is obtained by multiplying WQW^{Q} with this column vector:

WQ​(xq𝟎d)=(q1q2)​xq∈ℝD,W^{Q}\begin{pmatrix}x_{q}\\ \mathbf{0}_{d}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}q_{1}\\ q_{2}\end{pmatrix}x_{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{D}, (A13)

where we have used the partition of WQ=[q|∗]W^{Q}=[q|*] and q=(q1q2)q=\begin{pmatrix}q_{1}\\ q_{2}\end{pmatrix} as defined in Section A.2.

Next, we consider the term Γ^​WQ​Z=(Z​Z⊤N)​WQ​Z\hat{\Gamma}W^{Q}Z=\left(\frac{ZZ^{\top}}{N}\right)W^{Q}Z. The (N+1)(N+1)-th column of this product is obtained by multiplying the matrix Γ^\hat{\Gamma} with the (N+1)(N+1)-th column of WQ​ZW^{Q}Z, which we just computed in Equation (A13). Thus, the (N+1)(N+1)-th column of Γ^​WQ​Z\hat{\Gamma}W^{Q}Z is:

Γ^​(WQ​(xq𝟎d))=Γ^​(q1q2)​xq∈ℝD.\hat{\Gamma}\left(W^{Q}\begin{pmatrix}x_{q}\\ \mathbf{0}_{d}\end{pmatrix}\right)=\hat{\Gamma}\begin{pmatrix}q_{1}\\ q_{2}\end{pmatrix}x_{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{D}. (A14)

Now, we consider the term WP​Γ^​WQ​ZW^{P}\hat{\Gamma}W^{Q}Z. The (N+1)(N+1)-th column of this term is obtained by multiplying WPW^{P} with the vector in Equation (A14). Using the partition of WP=(∗pT)W^{P}=\begin{pmatrix}*\\ p^{T}\end{pmatrix} and pT=(p1p2)p^{T}=\begin{pmatrix}p_{1}&p_{2}\end{pmatrix} from Section A.2, we have:

WP​(Γ^​(q1q2)​xq)=(∗pT)​Γ^​(q1q2)​xq=(∗pT​Γ^​(q1q2)​xq)∈ℝD,W^{P}\left(\hat{\Gamma}\begin{pmatrix}q_{1}\\ q_{2}\end{pmatrix}x_{q}\right)=\begin{pmatrix}*\\ p^{T}\end{pmatrix}\hat{\Gamma}\begin{pmatrix}q_{1}\\ q_{2}\end{pmatrix}x_{q}=\begin{pmatrix}*\\ p^{T}\hat{\Gamma}\begin{pmatrix}q_{1}\\ q_{2}\end{pmatrix}x_{q}\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{D}, (A15)

where ∗* denotes the top dd rows of the resulting vector, which are not relevant for our prediction.

Finally, we look at the (N+1)(N+1)-th column of f⁡(Z)=Z+WP​Γ^​WQ​Zf(Z)=Z+W^{P}\hat{\Gamma}W^{Q}Z. This column is the sum of the (N+1)(N+1)-th column of ZZ and the (N+1)(N+1)-th column of WP​Γ^​WQ​ZW^{P}\hat{\Gamma}W^{Q}Z:

(xq𝟎d)+WP​Γ^​(q1q2)​xq=(xq𝟎d)+(∗pT​Γ^​(q1q2)​xq)=(∗𝟎d+pT​Γ^​(q1q2)​xq)∈ℝD.\begin{pmatrix}x_{q}\\ \mathbf{0}_{d}\end{pmatrix}+W^{P}\hat{\Gamma}\begin{pmatrix}q_{1}\\ q_{2}\end{pmatrix}x_{q}=\begin{pmatrix}x_{q}\\ \mathbf{0}_{d}\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}*\\ p^{T}\hat{\Gamma}\begin{pmatrix}q_{1}\\ q_{2}\end{pmatrix}x_{q}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}*\\ \mathbf{0}_{d}+p^{T}\hat{\Gamma}\begin{pmatrix}q_{1}\\ q_{2}\end{pmatrix}x_{q}\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{D}. (A16)

The prediction y^\hat{y} is the bottom dd elements of this resulting column. Thus, we have:

y^=𝟎d+pT​Γ^​(q1q2)​xq=pT​Γ^​(q1q2)​xq=(p1p2)​Γ^​(q1q2)​xq∈ℝd.\hat{y}=\mathbf{0}_{d}+p^{T}\hat{\Gamma}\begin{pmatrix}q_{1}\\ q_{2}\end{pmatrix}x_{q}=p^{T}\hat{\Gamma}\begin{pmatrix}q_{1}\\ q_{2}\end{pmatrix}x_{q}=\begin{pmatrix}p_{1}&p_{2}\end{pmatrix}\hat{\Gamma}\begin{pmatrix}q_{1}\\ q_{2}\end{pmatrix}x_{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. (A17)

Since q=(q1q2)q=\begin{pmatrix}q_{1}\\ q_{2}\end{pmatrix} and pT=(p1p2)p^{T}=\begin{pmatrix}p_{1}&p_{2}\end{pmatrix}, we can rewrite the prediction as:

y^=(pT​Γ^​q)​xq=((p1p2)​Γ^​(q1q2))​xq∈ℝd.\hat{y}=\left(p^{T}\hat{\Gamma}q\right)x_{q}=\left(\begin{pmatrix}p_{1}&p_{2}\end{pmatrix}\hat{\Gamma}\begin{pmatrix}q_{1}\\ q_{2}\end{pmatrix}\right)x_{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. (A18)

This matches the simplified predictor form given in Equation (A4).

For a specific regression task μ\mu, using the approximated empirical covariance matrix from Equation (A11), Γ^μ≈[Σ^xΣ^x​(Wμ)⊤Wμ​Σ^xWμ​Σ^x​(Wμ)⊤]\hat{\Gamma}^{\mu}\approx\begin{bmatrix}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}&\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top}\\ W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}&W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top}\end{bmatrix}, the prediction can be further expanded as:

y^μ\displaystyle\hat{y}_{\mu} =(pT​Γ^μ​q)​xq\displaystyle=\left(p^{T}\hat{\Gamma}^{\mu}q\right)x_{q}
=(p1p2)​[Σ^xΣ^x​(Wμ)⊤Wμ​Σ^xWμ​Σ^x​(Wμ)⊤]​(q1q2)​xq\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}p_{1}&p_{2}\end{pmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}&\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top}\\ W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}&W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top}\end{bmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}q_{1}\\ q_{2}\end{pmatrix}x_{q}
=(p1p2)​(Σ^x​q1+Σ^x​(Wμ)⊤​q2Wμ​Σ^x​q1+Wμ​Σ^x​(Wμ)⊤​q2)​xq\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}p_{1}&p_{2}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}q_{1}+\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top}q_{2}\\ W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}q_{1}+W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top}q_{2}\end{pmatrix}x_{q}
=(p1​(Σ^x​q1+Σ^x​(Wμ)⊤​q2)+p2​(Wμ​Σ^x​q1+Wμ​Σ^x​(Wμ)⊤​q2))​xq\displaystyle=\left(p_{1}(\hat{\Sigma}_{x}q_{1}+\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top}q_{2})+p_{2}(W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}q_{1}+W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top}q_{2})\right)x_{q}
=(p1​Σ^x​q1+p1​Σ^x​(Wμ)⊤​q2+p2​Wμ​Σ^x​q1+p2​Wμ​Σ^x​(Wμ)⊤​q2)​xq\displaystyle=\left(p_{1}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}q_{1}+p_{1}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top}q_{2}+p_{2}W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}q_{1}+p_{2}W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top}q_{2}\right)x_{q}
=((p1​Σ^x+p2​Wμ​Σ^x)​q1+(p1​Σ^x​(Wμ)⊤+p2​Wμ​Σ^x​(Wμ)⊤)​q2)​xq\displaystyle=\left((p_{1}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}+p_{2}W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x})q_{1}+(p_{1}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top}+p_{2}W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top})q_{2}\right)x_{q}
=((p1+p2​Wμ)​Σ^x​q1+(p1+p2​Wμ)​Σ^x​(Wμ)⊤​q2)​xq\displaystyle=\left((p_{1}+p_{2}W^{\mu})\hat{\Sigma}_{x}q_{1}+(p_{1}+p_{2}W^{\mu})\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top}q_{2}\right)x_{q}
=((p1+p2​Wμ)​Σ^x​(q1+(Wμ)⊤​q2))​xq.\displaystyle=\left((p_{1}+p_{2}W^{\mu})\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(q_{1}+(W^{\mu})^{\top}q_{2})\right)x_{q}.

Thus, for task μ\mu, the simplified predictor is given by:

y^μ=((p1+p2​Wμ)​Σ^x​(q1+(Wμ)⊤​q2))​xq∈ℝd.\hat{y}_{\mu}=\left((p_{1}+p_{2}W^{\mu})\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(q_{1}+(W^{\mu})^{\top}q_{2})\right)x_{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. (A19)

When we initialize p1=0p_{1}=0 and q2=0q_{2}=0, the predictor for task μ\mu further simplifies to:

y^μ=(p2​Wμ​Σ^x​q1)​xq∈ℝd.\hat{y}_{\mu}=\left(p_{2}W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}q_{1}\right)x_{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. (A20)

This simplified form will be used in the subsequent analysis of the learning dynamics.

A.10 Null Parameter Analysis

In this section, we demonstrate that with specific initial conditions, namely p1=0p_{1}=0 and q2=0q_{2}=0, the expected gradients with respect to p1p_{1} and q2q_{2} are zero at the beginning of training. This result justifies setting these parameters to zero throughout the training process, thereby simplifying the predictor.

Recall the loss function for a single task μ\mu is given by:

ℒμ=12​‖y^μ−yqμ‖22=12​‖(pT​Γ^μ​q)​xq−yqμ‖22,\mathcal{L}^{\mu}=\frac{1}{2}\|\hat{y}_{\mu}-y_{q}^{\mu}\|_{2}^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\left\|\left(p^{T}\hat{\Gamma}^{\mu}q\right)x_{q}-y_{q}^{\mu}\right\|_{2}^{2}, (A21)

and the simplified predictor is:

y^μ=(pT​Γ^μ​q)​xq=((p1p2)​Γ^μ​(q1q2))​xq=((p1+p2​Wμ)​Σ^x​(q1+(Wμ)⊤​q2))​xq,\hat{y}_{\mu}=\left(p^{T}\hat{\Gamma}^{\mu}q\right)x_{q}=\left(\begin{pmatrix}p_{1}&p_{2}\end{pmatrix}\hat{\Gamma}^{\mu}\begin{pmatrix}q_{1}\\ q_{2}\end{pmatrix}\right)x_{q}=\left((p_{1}+p_{2}W^{\mu})\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(q_{1}+(W^{\mu})^{\top}q_{2})\right)x_{q}, (A22)

where we have used the approximated empirical covariance matrix Γ^μ≈[Σ^xΣ^x​(Wμ)⊤Wμ​Σ^xWμ​Σ^x​(Wμ)⊤]\hat{\Gamma}^{\mu}\approx\begin{bmatrix}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}&\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top}\\ W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}&W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top}\end{bmatrix} and expanded the matrix product. For simplicity in gradient derivation, let us define an intermediate term Aμ∈ℝdA^{\mu}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} as:

Aμ=Σ^x​(q1+(Wμ)⊤​q2)​xq.A^{\mu}=\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(q_{1}+(W^{\mu})^{\top}q_{2})x_{q}. (A23)

Then the predictor can be written as:

y^μ=(p1+p2​Wμ)​Aμ.\hat{y}_{\mu}=(p_{1}+p_{2}W^{\mu})A^{\mu}. (A24)

And the loss function becomes:

ℒμ=12​‖(p1+p2​Wμ)​Aμ−Wμ​xq‖22.\mathcal{L}^{\mu}=\frac{1}{2}\|(p_{1}+p_{2}W^{\mu})A^{\mu}-W^{\mu}x_{q}\|_{2}^{2}. (A25)

A.10.1 Gradient with respect to p1p_{1}

To compute the gradient of ℒμ\mathcal{L}^{\mu} with respect to p1p_{1}, we use the chain rule. Let g⁡(p1)=(p1+p2​Wμ)​Aμ−Wμ​xqg(p_{1})=(p_{1}+p_{2}W^{\mu})A^{\mu}-W^{\mu}x_{q}. Then ℒμ=12​‖g⁡(p1)‖22=12​g​(p1)⊤​g​(p1)\mathcal{L}^{\mu}=\frac{1}{2}\|g(p_{1})\|_{2}^{2}=\frac{1}{2}g(p_{1})^{\top}g(p_{1}). The gradient is given by:

∂ℒμ∂p1=∂g⁡(p1)∂p1⊤​∂ℒμ∂g⁡(p1)=(∂g⁡(p1)∂p1)⊤​g​(p1).\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}^{\mu}}{\partial p_{1}}=\frac{\partial g(p_{1})}{\partial p_{1}}^{\top}\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}^{\mu}}{\partial g(p_{1})}=\left(\frac{\partial g(p_{1})}{\partial p_{1}}\right)^{\top}g(p_{1}). (A26)

We compute the derivative of g⁡(p1)g(p_{1}) with respect to p1p_{1}. Since p1∈ℝd×dp_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}, we consider the derivative with respect to p1p_{1} as a linear transformation.

∂g⁡(p1)∂p1=∂∂p1​[(p1+p2​Wμ)​Aμ−Wμ​xq]=∂∂p1​[p1​Aμ+p2​Wμ​Aμ−Wμ​xq]=Aμ⊤.\frac{\partial g(p_{1})}{\partial p_{1}}=\frac{\partial}{\partial p_{1}}\left[(p_{1}+p_{2}W^{\mu})A^{\mu}-W^{\mu}x_{q}\right]=\frac{\partial}{\partial p_{1}}\left[p_{1}A^{\mu}+p_{2}W^{\mu}A^{\mu}-W^{\mu}x_{q}\right]=A^{\mu\top}. (A27)

Substituting this and g⁡(p1)g(p_{1}) into Equation (A26), we get:

∂ℒμ∂p1=(Aμ)⊤​((p1+p2​Wμ)​Aμ−Wμ​xq).\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}^{\mu}}{\partial p_{1}}=(A^{\mu})^{\top}\left((p_{1}+p_{2}W^{\mu})A^{\mu}-W^{\mu}x_{q}\right). (A28)

Substituting back the expression for AμA^{\mu} from Equation (A23):

∂ℒμ∂p1=(Σ^x​(q1+(Wμ)⊤​q2)​xq)⊤​((p1+p2​Wμ)​Σ^x​(q1+(Wμ)⊤​q2)​xq−Wμ​xq).\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}^{\mu}}{\partial p_{1}}=\left(\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(q_{1}+(W^{\mu})^{\top}q_{2})x_{q}\right)^{\top}\left((p_{1}+p_{2}W^{\mu})\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(q_{1}+(W^{\mu})^{\top}q_{2})x_{q}-W^{\mu}x_{q}\right). (A29)

The change in p1p_{1} after one SGD update step, summing over all PP tasks, is:

Δp1=−λ∑μ=1P(Σ^x(q1+(Wμ)⊤q2)xq)⊤((p1+p2Wμ)Σ^x(q1+(Wμ)⊤q2)xq−Wμxq).\Delta p_{1}=-\lambda\sum_{\mu=1}^{P}\left(\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(q_{1}+(W^{\mu})^{\top}q_{2})x_{q}\right)^{\top}\left((p_{1}+p_{2}W^{\mu})\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(q_{1}+(W^{\mu})^{\top}q_{2})x_{q}-W^{\mu}x_{q}\right). (A30)

Now, we evaluate the expected update 𝔼W​[Δ​p1]\mathbb{E}_{W}[\Delta p_{1}] under the initial conditions p1=0p_{1}=0 and q2=0q_{2}=0. Substituting p1=0p_{1}=0 and q2=0q_{2}=0 into Equation (A30), we get:

Δp1=−λ∑μ=1P(Σ^x(q1+(Wμ)⊤0)xq)⊤((0+p2Wμ)Σ^x(q1+(Wμ)⊤0)xq−Wμxq).\Delta p_{1}=-\lambda\sum_{\mu=1}^{P}\left(\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(q_{1}+(W^{\mu})^{\top}0)x_{q}\right)^{\top}\left((0+p_{2}W^{\mu})\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(q_{1}+(W^{\mu})^{\top}0)x_{q}-W^{\mu}x_{q}\right). (A31)

Simplifying this expression:

Δ​p1\displaystyle\Delta p_{1} =−λ∑μ=1P(Σ^xq1xq)⊤(p2WμΣ^xq1xq−Wμxq)\displaystyle=-\lambda\sum_{\mu=1}^{P}\left(\hat{\Sigma}_{x}q_{1}x_{q}\right)^{\top}\left(p_{2}W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}q_{1}x_{q}-W^{\mu}x_{q}\right) (A32)
=−λ∑μ=1P(xq⊤q1⊤Σ^x⊤)(p2WμΣ^xq1xq−Wμxq)\displaystyle=-\lambda\sum_{\mu=1}^{P}\left(x_{q}^{\top}q_{1}^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}^{\top}\right)\left(p_{2}W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}q_{1}x_{q}-W^{\mu}x_{q}\right) (A33)
=−λ∑μ=1Pxq⊤q1⊤Σ^x(p2WμΣ^xq1xq−Wμxq)\displaystyle=-\lambda\sum_{\mu=1}^{P}x_{q}^{\top}q_{1}^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}\left(p_{2}W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}q_{1}x_{q}-W^{\mu}x_{q}\right) (A34)
=−λ∑μ=1P(xq⊤q1⊤Σ^xp2WμΣ^xq1xq−xq⊤q1⊤Σ^xWμxq)\displaystyle=-\lambda\sum_{\mu=1}^{P}\left(x_{q}^{\top}q_{1}^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}p_{2}W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}q_{1}x_{q}-x_{q}^{\top}q_{1}^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}W^{\mu}x_{q}\right) (A35)
=−λ∑μ=1Pxq⊤q1⊤Σ^xp2WμΣ^xq1xq+λ∑μ=1Pxq⊤q1⊤Σ^xWμxq.\displaystyle=-\lambda\sum_{\mu=1}^{P}x_{q}^{\top}q_{1}^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}p_{2}W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}q_{1}x_{q}+\lambda\sum_{\mu=1}^{P}x_{q}^{\top}q_{1}^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}W^{\mu}x_{q}. (A36)

Taking the expectation of Δ​p1\Delta p_{1} with respect to WW, and using the linearity of expectation:

𝔼W[Δp1]=−λ∑μ=1Pxq⊤q1⊤Σ^xp2𝔼W[Wμ]Σ^xq1xq+λ∑μ=1Pxq⊤q1⊤Σ^x𝔼W[Wμ]xq.\mathbb{E}_{W}[\Delta p_{1}]=-\lambda\sum_{\mu=1}^{P}x_{q}^{\top}q_{1}^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}p_{2}\mathbb{E}_{W}[W^{\mu}]\hat{\Sigma}_{x}q_{1}x_{q}+\lambda\sum_{\mu=1}^{P}x_{q}^{\top}q_{1}^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}\mathbb{E}_{W}[W^{\mu}]x_{q}. (A37)

Since we have 𝔼W​[Wμ]=0\mathbb{E}_{W}[W^{\mu}]=0 from Section A.8.2, both terms in Equation (A37) become zero:

𝔼W​[Δ​p1]=0.\mathbb{E}_{W}[\Delta p_{1}]=0. (A38)

Thus, the expected gradient of ℒμ\mathcal{L}^{\mu} with respect to p1p_{1} is zero when p1=0p_{1}=0 and q2=0q_{2}=0.

A.10.2 Gradient with respect to q2q_{2}

Now, we compute the gradient of ℒμ\mathcal{L}^{\mu} with respect to q2q_{2}. Using the chain rule again, we need to compute ∂y^μ∂q2\frac{\partial\hat{y}^{\mu}}{\partial q_{2}}. From Equation (A24), y^μ=(p1+p2​Wμ)​Aμ\hat{y}^{\mu}=(p_{1}+p_{2}W^{\mu})A^{\mu}, and from Equation (A23), Aμ=Σ^x​(q1+(Wμ)⊤​q2)​xqA^{\mu}=\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(q_{1}+(W^{\mu})^{\top}q_{2})x_{q}. Therefore,

∂y^μ∂q2\displaystyle\frac{\partial\hat{y}^{\mu}}{\partial q_{2}} =∂∂q2​[(p1+p2​Wμ)​Σ^x​(q1+(Wμ)⊤​q2)​xq]\displaystyle=\frac{\partial}{\partial q_{2}}\left[(p_{1}+p_{2}W^{\mu})\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(q_{1}+(W^{\mu})^{\top}q_{2})x_{q}\right] (A39)
=(p1+p2​Wμ)​Σ^x​∂∂q2​[(q1+(Wμ)⊤​q2)​xq]\displaystyle=(p_{1}+p_{2}W^{\mu})\hat{\Sigma}_{x}\frac{\partial}{\partial q_{2}}\left[(q_{1}+(W^{\mu})^{\top}q_{2})x_{q}\right] (A40)
=(p1+p2​Wμ)​Σ^x​∂∂q2​[q1​xq+(Wμ)⊤​q2​xq]\displaystyle=(p_{1}+p_{2}W^{\mu})\hat{\Sigma}_{x}\frac{\partial}{\partial q_{2}}\left[q_{1}x_{q}+(W^{\mu})^{\top}q_{2}x_{q}\right] (A41)
=(p1+p2​Wμ)​Σ^x​(Wμ)⊤​xq.\displaystyle=(p_{1}+p_{2}W^{\mu})\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top}x_{q}. (A42)

The gradient of the loss ℒμ\mathcal{L}^{\mu} with respect to q2q_{2} is then:

∂ℒμ∂q2\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}^{\mu}}{\partial q_{2}} =(∂y^μ∂q2)⊤​(y^μ−yqμ)\displaystyle=\left(\frac{\partial\hat{y}^{\mu}}{\partial q_{2}}\right)^{\top}(\hat{y}^{\mu}-y_{q}^{\mu}) (A43)
=((p1+p2​Wμ)​Σ^x​(Wμ)⊤​xq)⊤​((p1+p2​Wμ)​Σ^x​(q1+(Wμ)⊤​q2)​xq−Wμ​xq)\displaystyle=\left((p_{1}+p_{2}W^{\mu})\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top}x_{q}\right)^{\top}\left((p_{1}+p_{2}W^{\mu})\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(q_{1}+(W^{\mu})^{\top}q_{2})x_{q}-W^{\mu}x_{q}\right) (A44)
=xq⊤​(Wμ)​Σ^x⊤​(p1+p2​Wμ)⊤​((p1+p2​Wμ)​Σ^x​(q1+(Wμ)⊤​q2)​xq−Wμ​xq)\displaystyle=x_{q}^{\top}(W^{\mu})\hat{\Sigma}_{x}^{\top}(p_{1}+p_{2}W^{\mu})^{\top}\left((p_{1}+p_{2}W^{\mu})\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(q_{1}+(W^{\mu})^{\top}q_{2})x_{q}-W^{\mu}x_{q}\right) (A45)
=xq⊤​Wμ​Σ^x​(p1⊤+(p2​Wμ)⊤)​((p1+p2​Wμ)​Σ^x​(q1+(Wμ)⊤​q2)​xq−Wμ​xq),\displaystyle=x_{q}^{\top}W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(p_{1}^{\top}+(p_{2}W^{\mu})^{\top})\left((p_{1}+p_{2}W^{\mu})\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(q_{1}+(W^{\mu})^{\top}q_{2})x_{q}-W^{\mu}x_{q}\right), (A46)

assuming Σ^x\hat{\Sigma}_{x} and p1,p2,Wμp_{1},p_{2},W^{\mu} are matrices such that transpose operation distributes linearly. The change in q2q_{2} after one SGD update step, summing over all PP tasks, is:

Δq2=−λ∑μ=1Pxq⊤WμΣ^x(p1⊤+(p2Wμ)⊤)((p1+p2Wμ)Σ^x(q1+(Wμ)⊤q2)xq−Wμxq).\Delta q_{2}=-\lambda\sum_{\mu=1}^{P}x_{q}^{\top}W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(p_{1}^{\top}+(p_{2}W^{\mu})^{\top})\left((p_{1}+p_{2}W^{\mu})\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(q_{1}+(W^{\mu})^{\top}q_{2})x_{q}-W^{\mu}x_{q}\right). (A47)

Substituting p1=0p_{1}=0 and q2=0q_{2}=0 into Equation (A47), we get:

Δq2=−λ∑μ=1Pxq⊤WμΣ^x(0⊤+(p2Wμ)⊤)((0+p2Wμ)Σ^x(q1+(Wμ)⊤0)xq−Wμxq).\Delta q_{2}=-\lambda\sum_{\mu=1}^{P}x_{q}^{\top}W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(0^{\top}+(p_{2}W^{\mu})^{\top})\left((0+p_{2}W^{\mu})\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(q_{1}+(W^{\mu})^{\top}0)x_{q}-W^{\mu}x_{q}\right). (A48)

Simplifying this expression:

Δ​q2\displaystyle\Delta q_{2} =−λ∑μ=1Pxq⊤WμΣ^x(p2Wμ)⊤(p2WμΣ^xq1xq−Wμxq)\displaystyle=-\lambda\sum_{\mu=1}^{P}x_{q}^{\top}W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(p_{2}W^{\mu})^{\top}\left(p_{2}W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}q_{1}x_{q}-W^{\mu}x_{q}\right) (A49)
=−λ∑μ=1Pxq⊤WμΣ^x(Wμ)⊤p2⊤(p2WμΣ^xq1xq−Wμxq)\displaystyle=-\lambda\sum_{\mu=1}^{P}x_{q}^{\top}W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top}p_{2}^{\top}\left(p_{2}W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}q_{1}x_{q}-W^{\mu}x_{q}\right) (A50)
=−λ∑μ=1P(xq⊤WμΣ^x(Wμ)⊤p2⊤p2WμΣ^xq1xq−xq⊤WμΣ^x(Wμ)⊤p2⊤Wμxq)\displaystyle=-\lambda\sum_{\mu=1}^{P}\left(x_{q}^{\top}W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top}p_{2}^{\top}p_{2}W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}q_{1}x_{q}-x_{q}^{\top}W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top}p_{2}^{\top}W^{\mu}x_{q}\right) (A51)
=−λ∑μ=1Pxq⊤WμΣ^x(Wμ)⊤p2⊤p2WμΣ^xq1xq+λ∑μ=1Pxq⊤WμΣ^x(Wμ)⊤p2⊤Wμxq.\displaystyle=-\lambda\sum_{\mu=1}^{P}x_{q}^{\top}W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top}p_{2}^{\top}p_{2}W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}q_{1}x_{q}+\lambda\sum_{\mu=1}^{P}x_{q}^{\top}W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top}p_{2}^{\top}W^{\mu}x_{q}. (A52)

Taking the expectation of Δ​q2\Delta q_{2} with respect to WW:

𝔼W[Δq2]=−λ∑μ=1Pxq⊤𝔼W[WμΣ^x(Wμ)⊤p2⊤p2Wμ]Σ^xq1xq+λ∑μ=1Pxq⊤𝔼W[WμΣ^x(Wμ)⊤p2⊤Wμ]xq.\mathbb{E}_{W}[\Delta q_{2}]=-\lambda\sum_{\mu=1}^{P}x_{q}^{\top}\mathbb{E}_{W}[W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top}p_{2}^{\top}p_{2}W^{\mu}]\hat{\Sigma}_{x}q_{1}x_{q}+\lambda\sum_{\mu=1}^{P}x_{q}^{\top}\mathbb{E}_{W}[W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top}p_{2}^{\top}W^{\mu}]x_{q}. (A53)

Consider the term 𝔼W​[Wμ​Σ^x​(Wμ)⊤​p2⊤​p2​Wμ]\mathbb{E}_{W}[W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top}p_{2}^{\top}p_{2}W^{\mu}]. Since WμW^{\mu} has zero mean and its elements are sampled from a Gaussian distribution, any term involving the expectation of an odd number of elements of WμW^{\mu} will be zero. The term Wμ​Σ^x​(Wμ)⊤​p2⊤​p2​WμW^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top}p_{2}^{\top}p_{2}W^{\mu} involves a product of three instances of WμW^{\mu}. While Σ^x\hat{\Sigma}_{x} and p2p_{2} are constant with respect to the expectation over WμW^{\mu}, the expectation 𝔼W​[Wμ​Σ^x​(Wμ)⊤​p2⊤​p2​Wμ]\mathbb{E}_{W}[W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top}p_{2}^{\top}p_{2}W^{\mu}] is a tensor of order 4, and each component of this tensor is an expectation of a product of three elements from WμW^{\mu}. For a centered Gaussian distribution, all odd moments are zero. Therefore, 𝔼W​[Wμ​Σ^x​(Wμ)⊤​p2⊤​p2​Wμ]=0\mathbb{E}_{W}[W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top}p_{2}^{\top}p_{2}W^{\mu}]=0. Similarly, 𝔼W​[Wμ​Σ^x​(Wμ)⊤​p2⊤​Wμ]=0\mathbb{E}_{W}[W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top}p_{2}^{\top}W^{\mu}]=0. Thus,

𝔼W​[Δ​q2]=0.\mathbb{E}_{W}[\Delta q_{2}]=0. (A54)

Hence, the expected gradient of ℒμ\mathcal{L}^{\mu} with respect to q2q_{2} is also zero when p1=0p_{1}=0 and q2=0q_{2}=0.

A.10.3 Simplified Predictor with p1=0p_{1}=0 and q2=0q_{2}=0

Given that the expected gradients for p1p_{1} and q2q_{2} are zero at initialization and remain zero in expectation under SGD, we can fix p1=0p_{1}=0 and q2=0q_{2}=0 throughout the training. With these null parameters, the predictor from Equation (A19) simplifies to:

y^μ=((0+p2​Wμ)​Σ^x​(q1+(Wμ)⊤​0))​xq=(p2​Wμ​Σ^x​q1)​xq∈ℝd.\hat{y}_{\mu}=\left((0+p_{2}W^{\mu})\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(q_{1}+(W^{\mu})^{\top}0)\right)x_{q}=\left(p_{2}W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}q_{1}\right)x_{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. (A55)

This simplified predictor, which depends only on the parameters p2p_{2} and q1q_{1}, will be the focus of our subsequent analysis of the learning dynamics.

A.11 Learning Dynamics of Parameters p2p_{2} and q1q_{1}

In this section, we derive the stochastic gradient descent (SGD) update rules for the parameters p2p_{2} and q1q_{1}, and then transition to continuous-time dynamics to analyze the learning behavior. We will utilize the simplified predictor y^μ=(p2​Wμ​Σ^x​q1)​xq\hat{y}_{\mu}=(p_{2}W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}q_{1})x_{q} and the loss function ℒμ=12​‖p2​Wμ​Σ^x​q1​xq−Wμ​xq‖22\mathcal{L}^{\mu}=\frac{1}{2}\|p_{2}W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}q_{1}x_{q}-W^{\mu}x_{q}\|_{2}^{2}, which are valid under the initial conditions p1=0p_{1}=0 and q2=0q_{2}=0 maintained throughout training as justified in Section A.10.

A.11.1 SGD Update for p2p_{2}

The gradient of the loss function ℒμ\mathcal{L}^{\mu} with respect to p2p_{2} for a given task μ\mu is derived as follows. Let h⁡(p2)=p2​Wμ​Σ^x​q1​xq−Wμ​xqh(p_{2})=p_{2}W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}q_{1}x_{q}-W^{\mu}x_{q}. Then ℒμ=12​‖h⁡(p2)‖22=12​h​(p2)⊤​h​(p2)\mathcal{L}^{\mu}=\frac{1}{2}\|h(p_{2})\|_{2}^{2}=\frac{1}{2}h(p_{2})^{\top}h(p_{2}). The gradient is given by:

∇p2ℒμ=(∂h⁡(p2)∂p2)⊤​h​(p2).\nabla_{p_{2}}\mathcal{L}^{\mu}=\left(\frac{\partial h(p_{2})}{\partial p_{2}}\right)^{\top}h(p_{2}). (A56)

We compute the derivative of h⁡(p2)h(p_{2}) with respect to p2p_{2}:

∂h⁡(p2)∂p2=∂∂p2​[p2​Wμ​Σ^x​q1​xq−Wμ​xq]=∂∂p2​[p2​(Wμ​Σ^x​q1​xq)−Wμ​xq]=(Wμ​Σ^x​q1​xq)⊤=xq⊤​q1⊤​Σ^x⊤​(Wμ)⊤=xq⊤​q1⊤​Σ^x​(Wμ)⊤,\frac{\partial h(p_{2})}{\partial p_{2}}=\frac{\partial}{\partial p_{2}}\left[p_{2}W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}q_{1}x_{q}-W^{\mu}x_{q}\right]=\frac{\partial}{\partial p_{2}}\left[p_{2}(W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}q_{1}x_{q})-W^{\mu}x_{q}\right]=(W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}q_{1}x_{q})^{\top}=x_{q}^{\top}q_{1}^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}^{\top}(W^{\mu})^{\top}=x_{q}^{\top}q_{1}^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top}, (A57)

since Σ^x\hat{\Sigma}_{x} is symmetric. Substituting this into Equation (A56) and using h⁡(p2)=p2​Wμ​Σ^x​q1​xq−Wμ​xqh(p_{2})=p_{2}W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}q_{1}x_{q}-W^{\mu}x_{q}, we obtain the gradient:

∇p2ℒμ\displaystyle\nabla_{p_{2}}\mathcal{L}^{\mu} =(xq⊤​q1⊤​Σ^x​(Wμ)⊤)⊤​(p2​Wμ​Σ^x​q1​xq−Wμ​xq)\displaystyle=\left(x_{q}^{\top}q_{1}^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top}\right)^{\top}\left(p_{2}W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}q_{1}x_{q}-W^{\mu}x_{q}\right) (A58)
=(Wμ​Σ^x​q1​xq−Wμ​xq)​(xq⊤​q1⊤​Σ^x​(Wμ)⊤)\displaystyle=(W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}q_{1}x_{q}-W^{\mu}x_{q})\left(x_{q}^{\top}q_{1}^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top}\right) (A59)
=(p2​Wμ​Σ^x​q1​xq−Wμ​xq)​xq⊤​q1⊤​Σ^x​(Wμ)⊤.\displaystyle=\left(p_{2}W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}q_{1}x_{q}-W^{\mu}x_{q}\right)x_{q}^{\top}q_{1}^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top}. (A60)

The SGD update rule for p2p_{2} for a given task μ\mu is thus:

Δ​p2​(μ)\displaystyle\Delta p_{2}(\mu) =−λ​∇p2ℒμ\displaystyle=-\lambda\nabla_{p_{2}}\mathcal{L}_{\mu} (A61)
=−λ⁡(p2​Wμ​Σ^x​q1​xq−Wμ​xq)​xq⊤​q1⊤​Σ^x​(Wμ)⊤.\displaystyle=-\lambda\left(p_{2}W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}q_{1}x_{q}-W^{\mu}x_{q}\right)x_{q}^{\top}q_{1}^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top}. (A62)

Summing over all tasks μ=1,…,P\mu=1,\dots,P for one epoch update, we get:

Δ​p2\displaystyle\Delta p_{2} =∑μ=1PΔ​p2​(μ)\displaystyle=\sum_{\mu=1}^{P}\Delta p_{2}(\mu) (A63)
=−λ∑μ=1P(p2WμΣ^xq1xq−Wμxq)xq⊤q1⊤Σ^x(Wμ)⊤\displaystyle=-\lambda\sum_{\mu=1}^{P}\left(p_{2}W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}q_{1}x_{q}-W^{\mu}x_{q}\right)x_{q}^{\top}q_{1}^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top} (A64)
=−λ∑μ=1P(p2WμΣ^xq1xqxq⊤q1⊤Σ^x(Wμ)⊤−Wμxqxq⊤q1⊤Σ^x(Wμ)⊤).\displaystyle=-\lambda\sum_{\mu=1}^{P}\left(p_{2}W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}q_{1}x_{q}x_{q}^{\top}q_{1}^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top}-W^{\mu}x_{q}x_{q}^{\top}q_{1}^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}(W^{\mu})^{\top}\right). (A65)

A.11.2 Change of Variables and Assumptions for Tractable Dynamics

To simplify the analysis and derive tractable learning dynamics, we introduce a change of variables and make further assumptions. We consider the singular value decomposition of the population covariance matrix Σx\Sigma_{x} and the empirical covariance matrix Σ^x\hat{\Sigma}_{x} of the input data {xi}i=1N\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}:

Σx\displaystyle\Sigma_{x} =\displaystyle= U​S​U⊤,\displaystyle USU^{\top}, (A66)
Σ^x\displaystyle\hat{\Sigma}_{x} =\displaystyle= U​S^​U⊤,\displaystyle U\hat{S}U^{\top}, (A67)

where U∈ℝd×dU\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} is an orthogonal matrix, S=diag​(s1,…,sd)∈ℝd×dS=\text{diag}(s_{1},\dots,s_{d})\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} is a diagonal matrix of singular values of Σx\Sigma_{x}, and S^=diag​(s^1,…,s^d)∈ℝd×d\hat{S}=\text{diag}(\hat{s}_{1},\dots,\hat{s}_{d})\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} is a diagonal matrix related to the empirical singular values. We further assume that the orthogonal matrix VV used in the generation of the transformation matrices Wμ=V​Λμ​V⊤W^{\mu}=V\Lambda^{\mu}V^{\top} (Equation (A7)) is the same as UU, i.e., V=UV=U. Thus, we have Wμ=U​Λμ​U⊤W^{\mu}=U\Lambda^{\mu}U^{\top}.

We also assume that the parameters p2p_{2} and q1q_{1} are initialized and maintain the following form throughout training:

p2\displaystyle p_{2} =\displaystyle= U​p¯2​U⊤,\displaystyle U\bar{p}_{2}U^{\top}, (A68)
q1\displaystyle q_{1} =\displaystyle= U​q¯1​U⊤,\displaystyle U\bar{q}_{1}U^{\top}, (A69)

where p¯2\bar{p}_{2} and q¯1\bar{q}_{1} are diagonal matrices.

Substituting these decompositions into the update rule for Δ​p2\Delta p_{2} (Equation (A65)), and noting that (Wμ)⊤=(U​Λμ​U⊤)⊤=U​(Λμ)⊤​U⊤=U​Λμ​U⊤(W^{\mu})^{\top}=(U\Lambda^{\mu}U^{\top})^{\top}=U(\Lambda^{\mu})^{\top}U^{\top}=U\Lambda^{\mu}U^{\top} since Λμ\Lambda^{\mu} is a diagonal matrix, and similarly Σ^x⊤=Σ^x\hat{\Sigma}_{x}^{\top}=\hat{\Sigma}_{x}, we have:

Δ​p2\displaystyle\Delta p_{2} =−λ∑μ=1P((Up¯2U⊤)(UΛμU⊤)(US^U⊤)(Uq¯1U⊤)xqxq⊤(Uq¯1U⊤)⊤(US^U⊤)(UΛμU⊤)\displaystyle=-\lambda\sum_{\mu=1}^{P}\left((U\bar{p}_{2}U^{\top})(U\Lambda^{\mu}U^{\top})(U\hat{S}U^{\top})(U\bar{q}_{1}U^{\top})x_{q}x_{q}^{\top}(U\bar{q}_{1}U^{\top})^{\top}(U\hat{S}U^{\top})(U\Lambda^{\mu}U^{\top})\right.
OPEN−(U​Λμ​U⊤)​xq​xq⊤​(U​q¯1​U⊤)⊤​(U​S^​U⊤)​(U​Λμ​U⊤))\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\left.-(U\Lambda^{\mu}U^{\top})x_{q}x_{q}^{\top}(U\bar{q}_{1}U^{\top})^{\top}(U\hat{S}U^{\top})(U\Lambda^{\mu}U^{\top})\right)
=−λ∑μ=1P(Up¯2ΛμS^q¯1U⊤xqxq⊤Uq¯1S^ΛμU⊤−UΛμU⊤xqxq⊤Uq¯1S^ΛμU⊤),\displaystyle=-\lambda\sum_{\mu=1}^{P}\left(U\bar{p}_{2}\Lambda^{\mu}\hat{S}\bar{q}_{1}U^{\top}x_{q}x_{q}^{\top}U\bar{q}_{1}\hat{S}\Lambda^{\mu}U^{\top}-U\Lambda^{\mu}U^{\top}x_{q}x_{q}^{\top}U\bar{q}_{1}\hat{S}\Lambda^{\mu}U^{\top}\right),

using the orthogonality of UU, i.e., U⊤​U=U​U⊤=IU^{\top}U=UU^{\top}=I. We know that the change in p2p_{2} can also be decomposed as Δ​p2=p2​(t+1)−p2​(t)=U​p¯2​(t+1)​U⊤−U​p¯2​(t)​U⊤=U⁡(p¯2​(t+1)−p¯2​(t))​U⊤=U​Δ​p¯2​U⊤\Delta p_{2}=p_{2}(t+1)-p_{2}(t)=U\bar{p}_{2}(t+1)U^{\top}-U\bar{p}_{2}(t)U^{\top}=U(\bar{p}_{2}(t+1)-\bar{p}_{2}(t))U^{\top}=U\Delta\bar{p}_{2}U^{\top}. Thus, U​Δ​p¯2​U⊤U\Delta\bar{p}_{2}U^{\top} is equal to the expression above. Multiplying by U⊤U^{\top} from the left and UU from the right, and using orthogonality of UU, we get:

Δ​p¯2\displaystyle\Delta\bar{p}_{2} =−λ∑μ=1PU⊤(Up¯2ΛμS^q¯1U⊤xqxq⊤Uq¯1S^ΛμU⊤−UΛμU⊤xqxq⊤Uq¯1S^ΛμU⊤)U\displaystyle=-\lambda\sum_{\mu=1}^{P}U^{\top}\left(U\bar{p}_{2}\Lambda^{\mu}\hat{S}\bar{q}_{1}U^{\top}x_{q}x_{q}^{\top}U\bar{q}_{1}\hat{S}\Lambda^{\mu}U^{\top}-U\Lambda^{\mu}U^{\top}x_{q}x_{q}^{\top}U\bar{q}_{1}\hat{S}\Lambda^{\mu}U^{\top}\right)U
=−λ∑μ=1P(p¯2ΛμS^q¯1U⊤xqxq⊤Uq¯1S^Λμ−ΛμU⊤xqxq⊤Uq¯1S^Λμ).\displaystyle=-\lambda\sum_{\mu=1}^{P}\left(\bar{p}_{2}\Lambda^{\mu}\hat{S}\bar{q}_{1}U^{\top}x_{q}x_{q}^{\top}U\bar{q}_{1}\hat{S}\Lambda^{\mu}-\Lambda^{\mu}U^{\top}x_{q}x_{q}^{\top}U\bar{q}_{1}\hat{S}\Lambda^{\mu}\right).

Let x¯q=U⊤​xq\bar{x}_{q}=U^{\top}x_{q}. Then xq=U​x¯qx_{q}=U\bar{x}_{q} and U⊤​xq​xq⊤​U=U⊤​(U​x¯q)​(U​x¯q)⊤​U=U⊤​U​x¯q​x¯q⊤​U⊤​U=x¯q​x¯q⊤U^{\top}x_{q}x_{q}^{\top}U=U^{\top}(U\bar{x}_{q})(U\bar{x}_{q})^{\top}U=U^{\top}U\bar{x}_{q}\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}U^{\top}U=\bar{x}_{q}\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}. Thus,

Δ​p¯2\displaystyle\Delta\bar{p}_{2} =−λ∑μ=1P(p¯2ΛμS^q¯1x¯qx¯q⊤q¯1S^Λμ−Λμx¯qx¯q⊤q¯1S^Λμ)\displaystyle=-\lambda\sum_{\mu=1}^{P}\left(\bar{p}_{2}\Lambda^{\mu}\hat{S}\bar{q}_{1}\bar{x}_{q}\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}\bar{q}_{1}\hat{S}\Lambda^{\mu}-\Lambda^{\mu}\bar{x}_{q}\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}\bar{q}_{1}\hat{S}\Lambda^{\mu}\right) (A70)
=−λ∑μ=1P(p¯2ΛμS^2q¯12x¯qx¯q⊤Λμ−Λμ​2q¯1x¯qx¯q⊤S^),\displaystyle=-\lambda\sum_{\mu=1}^{P}\left(\bar{p}_{2}\Lambda^{\mu}\hat{S}^{2}\bar{q}_{1}^{2}\bar{x}_{q}\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}\Lambda^{\mu}-\Lambda^{\mu 2}\bar{q}_{1}\bar{x}_{q}\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}\hat{S}\right), (A71)

since S^\hat{S} and q¯1\bar{q}_{1} are diagonal matrices and commute.

Replacing the summation over tasks with expectation over Λ\Lambda, we get the expected update for p¯2\bar{p}_{2}:

𝔼Λ​[Δ​p¯2]=−λ​P​𝔼Λ​[p¯2​Λ​S^2​q¯12​x¯q​x¯q⊤​Λ−Λ2​q¯1​x¯q​x¯q⊤​S^].\mathbb{E}_{\Lambda}[\Delta\bar{p}_{2}]=-\lambda P\mathbb{E}_{\Lambda}\left[\bar{p}_{2}\Lambda\hat{S}^{2}\bar{q}_{1}^{2}\bar{x}_{q}\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}\Lambda-\Lambda^{2}\bar{q}_{1}\bar{x}_{q}\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}\hat{S}\right]. (A72)

Since all matrices in the expression are diagonal, they commute. Thus, we can rewrite Equation (A72) as:

𝔼Λ​[Δ​p¯2]=−λ​P​(p¯2​S^2​q¯12​x¯q​x¯q⊤​𝔼Λ​[Λ2]−𝔼Λ​[Λ2]​q¯1​x¯q​x¯q⊤​S^).\mathbb{E}_{\Lambda}[\Delta\bar{p}_{2}]=-\lambda P\left(\bar{p}_{2}\hat{S}^{2}\bar{q}_{1}^{2}\bar{x}_{q}\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}\mathbb{E}_{\Lambda}[\Lambda^{2}]-\mathbb{E}_{\Lambda}[\Lambda^{2}]\bar{q}_{1}\bar{x}_{q}\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}\hat{S}\right). (A73)

Given that the eigenvalues in Λ\Lambda are sampled from a standard multivariate Gaussian distribution, 𝔼⁡[Λ2]=I\mathbb{E}[\Lambda^{2}]=I. Substituting this into Equation (A73):

𝔼Λ​[Δ​p¯2]=−λ​P​(p¯2​S^2​q¯12​x¯q​x¯q⊤−q¯1​x¯q​x¯q⊤​S^).\mathbb{E}_{\Lambda}[\Delta\bar{p}_{2}]=-\lambda P\left(\bar{p}_{2}\hat{S}^{2}\bar{q}_{1}^{2}\bar{x}_{q}\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}-\bar{q}_{1}\bar{x}_{q}\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}\hat{S}\right). (A74)

Now, taking the expectation over x¯q​x¯q⊤\bar{x}_{q}\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}. Since xq∼𝒩⁡(0,Σx)x_{q}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma_{x}) and x¯q=U⊤​xq\bar{x}_{q}=U^{\top}x_{q}, we have x¯q∼𝒩⁡(0,U⊤​Σx​U)=𝒩⁡(0,S)\bar{x}_{q}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,U^{\top}\Sigma_{x}U)=\mathcal{N}(0,S). The expectation of x¯q​x¯q⊤\bar{x}_{q}\bar{x}_{q}^{\top} is 𝔼⁡[x¯q​x¯q⊤]=Cov​(x¯q)=S\mathbb{E}[\bar{x}_{q}\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}]=\text{Cov}(\bar{x}_{q})=S. Thus,

𝔼Λ,xq​[Δ​p¯2]=−λ​P​(p¯2​S^2​q¯12​S−q¯1​S​S^)=−λ​P​S​(p¯2​S^2​q¯12−q¯1​S^).\mathbb{E}_{\Lambda,x_{q}}[\Delta\bar{p}_{2}]=-\lambda P\left(\bar{p}_{2}\hat{S}^{2}\bar{q}_{1}^{2}S-\bar{q}_{1}S\hat{S}\right)=-\lambda PS\left(\bar{p}_{2}\hat{S}^{2}\bar{q}_{1}^{2}-\bar{q}_{1}\hat{S}\right). (A75)

Finally, we take the expectation over the empirical covariance matrix S^\hat{S}. We know that N​Σ^x=∑i=1Nxi​xi⊤N\hat{\Sigma}_{x}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}. If xi∼𝒩⁡(0,Σx)x_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma_{x}), then N​Σ^xN\hat{\Sigma}_{x} follows a Wishart distribution W⁡(N,Σx)W(N,\Sigma_{x}). In our diagonalized basis, N​S^=U⊤​(N​Σ^x)​UN\hat{S}=U^{\top}(N\hat{\Sigma}_{x})U also behaves like a Wishart matrix related to SS. For large NN, S^≈S\hat{S}\approx S. For expectation, we use the properties of Wishart distribution: 𝔼⁡[S^]=S\mathbb{E}[\hat{S}]=S and 𝔼⁡[S^2]=N+1N​S2+Tr⁡(S)​SN\mathbb{E}[\hat{S}^{2}]=\frac{N+1}{N}S^{2}+\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(S)S}{N}. Thus, taking expectation over S^\hat{S}:

𝔼⁡[Δ​p¯2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\Delta\bar{p}_{2}] =−λ​P​S​(p¯2​q¯12​𝔼​[S^2]−q¯1​𝔼​[S^])\displaystyle=-\lambda PS\left(\bar{p}_{2}\bar{q}_{1}^{2}\mathbb{E}[\hat{S}^{2}]-\bar{q}_{1}\mathbb{E}[\hat{S}]\right) (A76)
=−λ​P​S​(p¯2​q¯12​(N+1N​S2+Tr⁡(S)​SN)−q¯1​S)\displaystyle=-\lambda PS\left(\bar{p}_{2}\bar{q}_{1}^{2}\left(\frac{N+1}{N}S^{2}+\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(S)S}{N}\right)-\bar{q}_{1}S\right) (A77)
=−λ​P​S2​(p¯2​q¯12​(N+1N​S+Tr⁡(S)N​I)−q¯1​I).\displaystyle=-\lambda PS^{2}\left(\bar{p}_{2}\bar{q}_{1}^{2}\left(\frac{N+1}{N}S+\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(S)}{N}I\right)-\bar{q}_{1}I\right). (A78)

Due to the symmetry between p2p_{2} and q1q_{1} in the predictor structure and loss function, the derivation for the expected update of q¯1\bar{q}_{1}, 𝔼⁡[Δ​q¯1]\mathbb{E}[\Delta\bar{q}_{1}], will have a similar form with the roles of p¯2\bar{p}_{2} and q¯1\bar{q}_{1} interchanged. Therefore, by symmetry, we can write:

𝔼⁡[Δ​q¯1]=−λ​P​S2​(q¯1​p¯22​(N+1N​S+Tr⁡(S)N​I)−p¯2​I).\mathbb{E}[\Delta\bar{q}_{1}]=-\lambda PS^{2}\left(\bar{q}_{1}\bar{p}_{2}^{2}\left(\frac{N+1}{N}S+\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(S)}{N}I\right)-\bar{p}_{2}I\right). (A79)

A.11.3 Continuous-Time Dynamics

To analyze the learning dynamics in continuous time, we replace the discrete updates 𝔼⁡[Δ​p¯2]\mathbb{E}[\Delta\bar{p}_{2}] and 𝔼⁡[Δ​q¯1]\mathbb{E}[\Delta\bar{q}_{1}] with their continuous-time counterparts d​p¯2d​t\frac{d\bar{p}_{2}}{dt} and d​q¯1d​t\frac{d\bar{q}_{1}}{dt}, respectively. This leads to the following system of ordinary differential equations describing the learning dynamics:

d​p¯2d​t\displaystyle\frac{d\bar{p}_{2}}{dt} =−λ​P​S2​(p¯2​q¯12​(N+1N​S+Tr⁡(S)N​I)−q¯1​I),\displaystyle=-\lambda PS^{2}\left(\bar{p}_{2}\bar{q}_{1}^{2}\left(\frac{N+1}{N}S+\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(S)}{N}I\right)-\bar{q}_{1}I\right), (A80)
d​q¯1d​t\displaystyle\frac{d\bar{q}_{1}}{dt} =−λ​P​S2​(q¯1​p¯22​(N+1N​S+Tr⁡(S)N​I)−p¯2​I).\displaystyle=-\lambda PS^{2}\left(\bar{q}_{1}\bar{p}_{2}^{2}\left(\frac{N+1}{N}S+\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(S)}{N}I\right)-\bar{p}_{2}I\right). (A81)

Since p¯2\bar{p}_{2}, q¯1\bar{q}_{1}, and SS are diagonal matrices, these matrix equations decouple into dd independent systems of differential equations for the diagonal elements. Let sαs_{\alpha} be the α\alpha-th diagonal element of SS, pαp_{\alpha} be the α\alpha-th diagonal element of p¯2\bar{p}_{2}, and qαq_{\alpha} be the α\alpha-th diagonal element of q¯1\bar{q}_{1}. Then, for each dimension α=1,…,d\alpha=1,\dots,d, we have the dynamical equations:

d​pαd​t\displaystyle\frac{dp_{\alpha}}{dt} =−λ​P​sα2​(pα​qα2​(N+1N​sα+Tr⁡(S)N)−qα),\displaystyle=-\lambda Ps_{\alpha}^{2}\left(p_{\alpha}q_{\alpha}^{2}\left(\frac{N+1}{N}s_{\alpha}+\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(S)}{N}\right)-q_{\alpha}\right), (A82)
d​qαd​t\displaystyle\frac{dq_{\alpha}}{dt} =−λ​P​sα2​(qα​pα2​(N+1N​sα+Tr⁡(S)N)−pα).\displaystyle=-\lambda Ps_{\alpha}^{2}\left(q_{\alpha}p_{\alpha}^{2}\left(\frac{N+1}{N}s_{\alpha}+\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(S)}{N}\right)-p_{\alpha}\right). (A83)

These equations describe the continuous-time learning dynamics of the parameters pαp_{\alpha} and qαq_{\alpha} for each dimension α\alpha.

A.12 Dynamical Equations and Conserved Quantity

In this section, we analyze the continuous-time learning dynamics derived in Equations (A80) and (A81) and identify a conserved quantity associated with these dynamics. We then simplify these equations further by considering the diagonal elements and solve for the learning trajectory.

A.12.1 Conserved Quantity

An important observation regarding the learning dynamics is the existence of a conserved quantity, which remains constant throughout the training process. Let us define a quantity 𝒞\mathcal{C} as the difference of squared Frobenius norms of p¯2\bar{p}_{2} and q¯1\bar{q}_{1}:

𝒞=‖p¯2‖F2−‖q¯1‖F2=Tr​(p¯2⊤​p¯2)−Tr​(q¯1⊤​q¯1).\mathcal{C}=\|\bar{p}_{2}\|_{F}^{2}-\|\bar{q}_{1}\|_{F}^{2}=\text{Tr}(\bar{p}_{2}^{\top}\bar{p}_{2})-\text{Tr}(\bar{q}_{1}^{\top}\bar{q}_{1}). (A84)

Since p¯2\bar{p}_{2} and q¯1\bar{q}_{1} are diagonal matrices, ‖p¯2‖F2=∑αpα2\|\bar{p}_{2}\|_{F}^{2}=\sum_{\alpha}p_{\alpha}^{2} and ‖q¯1‖F2=∑αqα2\|\bar{q}_{1}\|_{F}^{2}=\sum_{\alpha}q_{\alpha}^{2}, where pαp_{\alpha} and qαq_{\alpha} are the diagonal elements. Thus, 𝒞=∑α(pα2−qα2)\mathcal{C}=\sum_{\alpha}(p_{\alpha}^{2}-q_{\alpha}^{2}).

To show that 𝒞\mathcal{C} is conserved, we compute its time derivative d​𝒞d​t\frac{d\mathcal{C}}{dt} using the chain rule and the dynamical equations for d​p¯2d​t\frac{d\bar{p}_{2}}{dt} and d​q¯1d​t\frac{d\bar{q}_{1}}{dt} (Equations (A80) and (A81)):

d​𝒞d​t\displaystyle\frac{d\mathcal{C}}{dt} =dd​t​(‖p¯2‖F2−‖q¯1‖F2)\displaystyle=\frac{d}{dt}\left(\|\bar{p}_{2}\|_{F}^{2}-\|\bar{q}_{1}\|_{F}^{2}\right)
=dd​t​Tr​(p¯2⊤​p¯2)−dd​t​Tr​(q¯1⊤​q¯1)\displaystyle=\frac{d}{dt}\text{Tr}(\bar{p}_{2}^{\top}\bar{p}_{2})-\frac{d}{dt}\text{Tr}(\bar{q}_{1}^{\top}\bar{q}_{1})
=2​Tr​(p¯2⊤​d​p¯2d​t)−2​Tr​(q¯1⊤​d​q¯1d​t)\displaystyle=2\text{Tr}\left(\bar{p}_{2}^{\top}\frac{d\bar{p}_{2}}{dt}\right)-2\text{Tr}\left(\bar{q}_{1}^{\top}\frac{d\bar{q}_{1}}{dt}\right)
=2​Tr​(p¯2​d​p¯2d​t)−2​Tr​(q¯1​d​q¯1d​t),\displaystyle=2\text{Tr}\left(\bar{p}_{2}\frac{d\bar{p}_{2}}{dt}\right)-2\text{Tr}\left(\bar{q}_{1}\frac{d\bar{q}_{1}}{dt}\right),

since for diagonal matrices p¯2⊤=p¯2\bar{p}_{2}^{\top}=\bar{p}_{2} and q¯1⊤=q¯1\bar{q}_{1}^{\top}=\bar{q}_{1}. Substituting the expressions for d​p¯2d​t\frac{d\bar{p}_{2}}{dt} and d​q¯1d​t\frac{d\bar{q}_{1}}{dt} from Equations (A80) and (A81):

d​𝒞d​t\displaystyle\frac{d\mathcal{C}}{dt} =2​Tr​[p¯2​(−λ​P​S2​(p¯2​q¯12​(N+1N​S+Tr⁡(S)N​I)−q¯1​I))]\displaystyle=2\text{Tr}\left[\bar{p}_{2}\left(-\lambda PS^{2}\left(\bar{p}_{2}\bar{q}_{1}^{2}\left(\frac{N+1}{N}S+\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(S)}{N}I\right)-\bar{q}_{1}I\right)\right)\right]
−2​Tr​[q¯1​(−λ​P​S2​(q¯1​p¯22​(N+1N​S+Tr⁡(S)N​I)−p¯2​I))]\displaystyle\quad-2\text{Tr}\left[\bar{q}_{1}\left(-\lambda PS^{2}\left(\bar{q}_{1}\bar{p}_{2}^{2}\left(\frac{N+1}{N}S+\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(S)}{N}I\right)-\bar{p}_{2}I\right)\right)\right]
=−2​λ​P​Tr​[S2​p¯2​(p¯2​q¯12​(N+1N​S+Tr⁡(S)N​I)−q¯1​I)]\displaystyle=-2\lambda P\text{Tr}\left[S^{2}\bar{p}_{2}\left(\bar{p}_{2}\bar{q}_{1}^{2}\left(\frac{N+1}{N}S+\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(S)}{N}I\right)-\bar{q}_{1}I\right)\right]
+2​λ​P​Tr​[S2​q¯1​(q¯1​p¯22​(N+1N​S+Tr⁡(S)N​I)−p¯2​I)]\displaystyle\quad+2\lambda P\text{Tr}\left[S^{2}\bar{q}_{1}\left(\bar{q}_{1}\bar{p}_{2}^{2}\left(\frac{N+1}{N}S+\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(S)}{N}I\right)-\bar{p}_{2}I\right)\right]
=−2​λ​P​Tr​[S2​p¯22​q¯12​(N+1N​S+Tr⁡(S)N​I)−S2​p¯2​q¯1​I]\displaystyle=-2\lambda P\text{Tr}\left[S^{2}\bar{p}_{2}^{2}\bar{q}_{1}^{2}\left(\frac{N+1}{N}S+\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(S)}{N}I\right)-S^{2}\bar{p}_{2}\bar{q}_{1}I\right]
+2​λ​P​Tr​[S2​q¯12​p¯22​(N+1N​S+Tr⁡(S)N​I)−S2​q¯1​p¯2​I].\displaystyle\quad+2\lambda P\text{Tr}\left[S^{2}\bar{q}_{1}^{2}\bar{p}_{2}^{2}\left(\frac{N+1}{N}S+\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(S)}{N}I\right)-S^{2}\bar{q}_{1}\bar{p}_{2}I\right].

Since matrix trace is linear and cyclic, and all matrices here are diagonal and thus commute, we have Tr​[S2​p¯22​q¯12​(⋅)]=Tr​[S2​q¯12​p¯22​(⋅)]\text{Tr}[S^{2}\bar{p}_{2}^{2}\bar{q}_{1}^{2}(\cdot)]=\text{Tr}[S^{2}\bar{q}_{1}^{2}\bar{p}_{2}^{2}(\cdot)] and Tr​[S2​p¯2​q¯1​I]=Tr​[S2​q¯1​p¯2​I]\text{Tr}[S^{2}\bar{p}_{2}\bar{q}_{1}I]=\text{Tr}[S^{2}\bar{q}_{1}\bar{p}_{2}I]. Therefore, the terms cancel out exactly:

d​𝒞d​t=0.\frac{d\mathcal{C}}{dt}=0.

This shows that 𝒞=‖p¯2‖F2−‖q¯1‖F2\mathcal{C}=\|\bar{p}_{2}\|_{F}^{2}-\|\bar{q}_{1}\|_{F}^{2} is indeed a conserved quantity of the learning dynamics.

A.12.2 Diagonal Element Dynamics and Solution

As noted earlier, the matrix dynamical equations decouple into dd independent systems for the diagonal elements. For each dimension α=1,…,d\alpha=1,\dots,d, the dynamical equations are given by Equations (A82) and (A83):

d​pαd​t\displaystyle\frac{dp_{\alpha}}{dt} =−λ​P​sα2​(pα​qα2​(N+1N​sα+Tr⁡(S)N)−qα),\displaystyle=-\lambda Ps_{\alpha}^{2}\left(p_{\alpha}q_{\alpha}^{2}\left(\frac{N+1}{N}s_{\alpha}+\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(S)}{N}\right)-q_{\alpha}\right), (A85)
d​qαd​t\displaystyle\frac{dq_{\alpha}}{dt} =−λ​P​sα2​(qα​pα2​(N+1N​sα+Tr⁡(S)N)−pα).\displaystyle=-\lambda Ps_{\alpha}^{2}\left(q_{\alpha}p_{\alpha}^{2}\left(\frac{N+1}{N}s_{\alpha}+\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(S)}{N}\right)-p_{\alpha}\right). (A86)

Let us define a term sα∞=(N+1N​sα+Tr⁡(S)N)s_{\alpha}^{\infty}=\left(\frac{N+1}{N}s_{\alpha}+\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(S)}{N}\right). Then the dynamical equations can be rewritten as:

d​pαd​t\displaystyle\frac{dp_{\alpha}}{dt} =−λ​P​sα2​(pα​qα2​sα∞−qα)=λ​P​sα2​qα​(1−pα​qα​sα∞),\displaystyle=-\lambda Ps_{\alpha}^{2}\left(p_{\alpha}q_{\alpha}^{2}s_{\alpha}^{\infty}-q_{\alpha}\right)=\lambda Ps_{\alpha}^{2}q_{\alpha}\left(1-p_{\alpha}q_{\alpha}s_{\alpha}^{\infty}\right), (A87)
d​qαd​t\displaystyle\frac{dq_{\alpha}}{dt} =−λ​P​sα2​(qα​pα2​sα∞−pα)=λ​P​sα2​pα​(1−pα​qα​sα∞).\displaystyle=-\lambda Ps_{\alpha}^{2}\left(q_{\alpha}p_{\alpha}^{2}s_{\alpha}^{\infty}-p_{\alpha}\right)=\lambda Ps_{\alpha}^{2}p_{\alpha}\left(1-p_{\alpha}q_{\alpha}s_{\alpha}^{\infty}\right). (A88)

We define an effective timescale for learning in each dimension α\alpha as τα=1λ​P​sα2\tau_{\alpha}=\frac{1}{\lambda Ps_{\alpha}^{2}}. Then, the dynamics become:

τα​d​pαd​t\displaystyle\tau_{\alpha}\frac{dp_{\alpha}}{dt} =qα​(1−pα​qα​sα∞),\displaystyle=q_{\alpha}\left(1-p_{\alpha}q_{\alpha}s_{\alpha}^{\infty}\right), (A89)
τα​d​qαd​t\displaystyle\tau_{\alpha}\frac{dq_{\alpha}}{dt} =pα​(1−pα​qα​sα∞).\displaystyle=p_{\alpha}\left(1-p_{\alpha}q_{\alpha}s_{\alpha}^{\infty}\right). (A90)

Observe that τα​pα​d​pαd​t=pα​qα​(1−pα​qα​sα∞)\tau_{\alpha}p_{\alpha}\frac{dp_{\alpha}}{dt}=p_{\alpha}q_{\alpha}\left(1-p_{\alpha}q_{\alpha}s_{\alpha}^{\infty}\right) and τα​qα​d​qαd​t=pα​qα​(1−pα​qα​sα∞)\tau_{\alpha}q_{\alpha}\frac{dq_{\alpha}}{dt}=p_{\alpha}q_{\alpha}\left(1-p_{\alpha}q_{\alpha}s_{\alpha}^{\infty}\right). Thus, τα​pα​d​pαd​t=τα​qα​d​qαd​t\tau_{\alpha}p_{\alpha}\frac{dp_{\alpha}}{dt}=\tau_{\alpha}q_{\alpha}\frac{dq_{\alpha}}{dt}, which implies pα​d​pαd​t=qα​d​qαd​tp_{\alpha}\frac{dp_{\alpha}}{dt}=q_{\alpha}\frac{dq_{\alpha}}{dt}, or pα​d​pα=qα​d​qαp_{\alpha}dp_{\alpha}=q_{\alpha}dq_{\alpha}. Integrating both sides, we get ∫pα​d​pα=∫qα​d​qα\int p_{\alpha}dp_{\alpha}=\int q_{\alpha}dq_{\alpha}, leading to 12​pα2=12​qα2+Cα′\frac{1}{2}p_{\alpha}^{2}=\frac{1}{2}q_{\alpha}^{2}+C^{\prime}_{\alpha}, or pα2−qα2=Cαp_{\alpha}^{2}-q_{\alpha}^{2}=C_{\alpha}, where Cα=2​Cα′C_{\alpha}=2C^{\prime}_{\alpha} is a constant of integration. This is the element-wise conserved quantity, consistent with the matrix conserved quantity 𝒞\mathcal{C}. If initialized with pα​(0)=qα​(0)p_{\alpha}(0)=q_{\alpha}(0), then Cα=0C_{\alpha}=0, and pα2​(t)=qα2​(t)p_{\alpha}^{2}(t)=q_{\alpha}^{2}(t) for all tt. aα​(t)\displaystyle a_{\alpha}(t) =aα01−aα0​sα∞​e2​tτα1+aα0​sα∞1−aα0​sα∞​e2​tτα=aα0​e2​tτα(1−aα0​sα∞)+aα0​sα∞​e2​tτα\displaystyle=\frac{\frac{a_{\alpha}^{0}}{1-a_{\alpha}^{0}s_{\alpha}^{\infty}}e^{\frac{2t}{\tau_{\alpha}}}}{1+\frac{a_{\alpha}^{0}s_{\alpha}^{\infty}}{1-a_{\alpha}^{0}s_{\alpha}^{\infty}}e^{\frac{2t}{\tau_{\alpha}}}}=\frac{a_{\alpha}^{0}e^{\frac{2t}{\tau_{\alpha}}}}{(1-a_{\alpha}^{0}s_{\alpha}^{\infty})+a_{\alpha}^{0}s_{\alpha}^{\infty}e^{\frac{2t}{\tau_{\alpha}}}}
=aα0(1−aα0​sα∞)​e−2​tτα+aα0​sα∞=aα0/sα∞((1−aα0​sα∞)/sα∞)​e−2​tτα+aα0\displaystyle=\frac{a_{\alpha}^{0}}{(1-a_{\alpha}^{0}s_{\alpha}^{\infty})e^{-\frac{2t}{\tau_{\alpha}}}+a_{\alpha}^{0}s_{\alpha}^{\infty}}=\frac{a_{\alpha}^{0}/s_{\alpha}^{\infty}}{((1-a_{\alpha}^{0}s_{\alpha}^{\infty})/s_{\alpha}^{\infty})e^{-\frac{2t}{\tau_{\alpha}}}+a_{\alpha}^{0}}
=aα0/sα∞(1sα∞−aα0)​e−2​tτα+aα0=aα∞​aα0(aα∞−aα0)​e−2​tτα+aα0\displaystyle=\frac{a_{\alpha}^{0}/s_{\alpha}^{\infty}}{(\frac{1}{s_{\alpha}^{\infty}}-a_{\alpha}^{0})e^{-\frac{2t}{\tau_{\alpha}}}+a_{\alpha}^{0}}=\frac{a_{\alpha}^{\infty}a_{\alpha}^{0}}{(a_{\alpha}^{\infty}-a_{\alpha}^{0})e^{-\frac{2t}{\tau_{\alpha}}}+a_{\alpha}^{0}}
=aα∞​aα0aα0+(aα∞−aα0)​e−2​tτα.\displaystyle=a_{\alpha}^{\infty}\frac{a_{\alpha}^{0}}{a_{\alpha}^{0}+(a_{\alpha}^{\infty}-a_{\alpha}^{0})e^{-\frac{2t}{\tau_{\alpha}}}}.

Thus, the solution for aα​(t)a_{\alpha}(t) is:

aα​(t)=aα∞​(aα0aα0+(aα∞−aα0)​exp⁡(−2​tτα)).a_{\alpha}(t)=a_{\alpha}^{\infty}\left(\frac{a_{\alpha}^{0}}{a_{\alpha}^{0}+\left(a_{\alpha}^{\infty}-a_{\alpha}^{0}\right)\exp\left(-\frac{2t}{\tau_{\alpha}}\right)}\right). (A91)

For small initial values aα0≈ϵa_{\alpha}^{0}\approx\epsilon and approaching the fixed point aα​(t)≈aα∞​(1−ϵ)a_{\alpha}(t)\approx a_{\alpha}^{\infty}(1-\epsilon), the time tt required to reach close to the fixed point can be approximated by solving for tt in:

ϵ\displaystyle\epsilon ≈(aα∞−aα0)​exp⁡(−2​tτα)\displaystyle\approx\left(a_{\alpha}^{\infty}-a_{\alpha}^{0}\right)\exp\left(-\frac{2t}{\tau_{\alpha}}\right)
exp⁡(2​tτα)\displaystyle\exp\left(\frac{2t}{\tau_{\alpha}}\right) ≈aα∞−aα0ϵ≈aα∞ϵ=1sα∞​ϵ\displaystyle\approx\frac{a_{\alpha}^{\infty}-a_{\alpha}^{0}}{\epsilon}\approx\frac{a_{\alpha}^{\infty}}{\epsilon}=\frac{1}{s_{\alpha}^{\infty}\epsilon}
2​tτα\displaystyle\frac{2t}{\tau_{\alpha}} ≈log⁡(1sα∞​ϵ)\displaystyle\approx\log\left(\frac{1}{s_{\alpha}^{\infty}\epsilon}\right)
t\displaystyle t ≈τα2​log⁡(1sα∞​ϵ)=12​λ​P​sα2​log⁡(1sα∞​ϵ).\displaystyle\approx\frac{\tau_{\alpha}}{2}\log\left(\frac{1}{s_{\alpha}^{\infty}\epsilon}\right)=\frac{1}{2\lambda Ps_{\alpha}^{2}}\log\left(\frac{1}{s_{\alpha}^{\infty}\epsilon}\right).

This gives an estimate of the convergence time for each dimension α\alpha.

A.13 Loss Analysis

In this section, we analyze the expected loss function of the linear transformer model. We first express the average loss per epoch and then simplify it using the change of variables and assumptions introduced in Section A.11. We will derive the expected loss in terms of the diagonal parameters aα​(t)a_{\alpha}(t) and analyze the loss behavior as training progresses.

A.13.1 Expected Loss Formulation

The loss function for a single task μ\mu is given by:

ℒμ=12​‖y^μ−yqμ‖22=12​‖p2​Wμ​Σ^x​q1​xq−Wμ​xq‖22.\mathcal{L}^{\mu}=\frac{1}{2}\|\hat{y}_{\mu}-y_{q}^{\mu}\|_{2}^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\|p_{2}W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}q_{1}x_{q}-W^{\mu}x_{q}\|_{2}^{2}. (A92)

The average loss per epoch over all PP tasks is:

ℒ=1P​∑μ=1Pℒμ=12​P​∑μ=1P‖p2​Wμ​Σ^x​q1​xq−Wμ​xq‖22.\mathcal{L}=\frac{1}{P}\sum_{\mu=1}^{P}\mathcal{L}^{\mu}=\frac{1}{2P}\sum_{\mu=1}^{P}\|p_{2}W^{\mu}\hat{\Sigma}_{x}q_{1}x_{q}-W^{\mu}x_{q}\|_{2}^{2}. (A93)

Replacing the summation with expectation over the distribution of WW and xqx_{q}, we obtain the expected loss:

ℒ=12​𝔼W,xq​[‖p2​W​Σ^x​q1​xq−W​xq‖22].\mathcal{L}=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{W,x_{q}}\left[\|p_{2}W\hat{\Sigma}_{x}q_{1}x_{q}-Wx_{q}\|_{2}^{2}\right]. (A94)

Using the change of variables p2=U​p¯2​U⊤p_{2}=U\bar{p}_{2}U^{\top}, q1=U​q¯1​U⊤q_{1}=U\bar{q}_{1}U^{\top}, W=U​Λ​U⊤W=U\Lambda U^{\top}, Σ^x=U​S^​U⊤\hat{\Sigma}_{x}=U\hat{S}U^{\top}, and xq=U​x¯qx_{q}=U\bar{x}_{q}, the expected loss becomes:

ℒ\displaystyle\mathcal{L} =12​𝔼Λ,x¯q​[‖(U​p¯2​U⊤)​(U​Λ​U⊤)​(U​S^​U⊤)​(U​q¯1​U⊤)​(U​x¯q)−(U​Λ​U⊤)​(U​x¯q)‖22]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{\Lambda,\bar{x}_{q}}\left[\|(U\bar{p}_{2}U^{\top})(U\Lambda U^{\top})(U\hat{S}U^{\top})(U\bar{q}_{1}U^{\top})(U\bar{x}_{q})-(U\Lambda U^{\top})(U\bar{x}_{q})\|_{2}^{2}\right] (A95)
=12​𝔼Λ,x¯q​[‖U​p¯2​Λ​S^​q¯1​x¯q−U​Λ​x¯q‖22]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{\Lambda,\bar{x}_{q}}\left[\|U\bar{p}_{2}\Lambda\hat{S}\bar{q}_{1}\bar{x}_{q}-U\Lambda\bar{x}_{q}\|_{2}^{2}\right] (A96)
=12​𝔼Λ,x¯q​[‖U⁡(p¯2​Λ​S^​q¯1​x¯q−Λ​x¯q)‖22].\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{\Lambda,\bar{x}_{q}}\left[\|U(\bar{p}_{2}\Lambda\hat{S}\bar{q}_{1}\bar{x}_{q}-\Lambda\bar{x}_{q})\|_{2}^{2}\right]. (A97)

Since the Euclidean norm is invariant under orthogonal transformations, ‖U​v‖2=‖v‖2\|Uv\|_{2}=\|v\|_{2} for any vector vv and orthogonal matrix UU. Thus, Equation (A97) simplifies to:

ℒ=12​𝔼Λ,x¯q​[‖p¯2​Λ​S^​q¯1​x¯q−Λ​x¯q‖22].\mathcal{L}=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{\Lambda,\bar{x}_{q}}\left[\|\bar{p}_{2}\Lambda\hat{S}\bar{q}_{1}\bar{x}_{q}-\Lambda\bar{x}_{q}\|_{2}^{2}\right]. (A98)

Under the assumption that pα​(t)=qα​(t)p_{\alpha}(t)=q_{\alpha}(t), we have p¯2=q¯1=a¯1/2\bar{p}_{2}=\bar{q}_{1}=\bar{a}^{1/2}, where a¯=diag​(a1,…,ad)\bar{a}=\text{diag}(a_{1},\dots,a_{d}). Then p¯2​q¯1=a¯\bar{p}_{2}\bar{q}_{1}=\bar{a}. The expected loss becomes:

ℒ=12​𝔼Λ,x¯q​[‖a¯​Λ​S^​x¯q−Λ​x¯q‖22].\mathcal{L}=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{\Lambda,\bar{x}_{q}}\left[\|\bar{a}\Lambda\hat{S}\bar{x}_{q}-\Lambda\bar{x}_{q}\|_{2}^{2}\right]. (A99)

A.13.2 Expansion and Term-wise Expectation

Expanding the squared norm in Equation (A99), we get:

ℒ\displaystyle\mathcal{L} =12​𝔼Λ,x¯q​[(a¯​Λ​S^​x¯q−Λ​x¯q)⊤​(a¯​Λ​S^​x¯q−Λ​x¯q)]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{\Lambda,\bar{x}_{q}}\left[(\bar{a}\Lambda\hat{S}\bar{x}_{q}-\Lambda\bar{x}_{q})^{\top}(\bar{a}\Lambda\hat{S}\bar{x}_{q}-\Lambda\bar{x}_{q})\right] (A100)
=12​𝔼Λ,x¯q​[(x¯q⊤​S^​Λ​a¯−x¯q⊤​Λ)​(a¯​Λ​S^​x¯q−Λ​x¯q)]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{\Lambda,\bar{x}_{q}}\left[(\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}\hat{S}\Lambda\bar{a}-\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}\Lambda)(\bar{a}\Lambda\hat{S}\bar{x}_{q}-\Lambda\bar{x}_{q})\right] (A101)
=12​𝔼Λ,x¯q​[x¯q⊤​S^​Λ​a¯2​Λ​S^​x¯q−x¯q⊤​S^​Λ​a¯​Λ​x¯q−x¯q⊤​Λ​a¯​Λ​S^​x¯q+x¯q⊤​Λ2​x¯q]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{\Lambda,\bar{x}_{q}}\left[\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}\hat{S}\Lambda\bar{a}^{2}\Lambda\hat{S}\bar{x}_{q}-\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}\hat{S}\Lambda\bar{a}\Lambda\bar{x}_{q}-\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}\Lambda\bar{a}\Lambda\hat{S}\bar{x}_{q}+\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}\Lambda^{2}\bar{x}_{q}\right] (A102)
=12​𝔼Λ,x¯q​[x¯q⊤​S^​Λ​a¯2​Λ​S^​x¯q−2​x¯q⊤​S^​Λ​a¯​Λ​x¯q+x¯q⊤​Λ2​x¯q],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{\Lambda,\bar{x}_{q}}\left[\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}\hat{S}\Lambda\bar{a}^{2}\Lambda\hat{S}\bar{x}_{q}-2\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}\hat{S}\Lambda\bar{a}\Lambda\bar{x}_{q}+\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}\Lambda^{2}\bar{x}_{q}\right], (A103)

where we used the fact that x¯q⊤​S^​Λ​a¯​Λ​x¯q=(x¯q⊤​S^​Λ​a¯​Λ​x¯q)⊤=x¯q⊤​Λ⊤​a¯⊤​Λ⊤​S^⊤​x¯q=x¯q⊤​Λ​a¯​Λ​S^​x¯q\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}\hat{S}\Lambda\bar{a}\Lambda\bar{x}_{q}=(\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}\hat{S}\Lambda\bar{a}\Lambda\bar{x}_{q})^{\top}=\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}\Lambda^{\top}\bar{a}^{\top}\Lambda^{\top}\hat{S}^{\top}\bar{x}_{q}=\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}\Lambda\bar{a}\Lambda\hat{S}\bar{x}_{q} since all matrices are diagonal and symmetric. We can analyze each term separately using trace operator and properties of expectation. Let E1=𝔼⁡[x¯q⊤​S^​Λ​a¯2​Λ​S^​x¯q]E_{1}=\mathbb{E}[\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}\hat{S}\Lambda\bar{a}^{2}\Lambda\hat{S}\bar{x}_{q}], E2=𝔼⁡[x¯q⊤​S^​Λ​a¯​Λ​x¯q]E_{2}=\mathbb{E}[\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}\hat{S}\Lambda\bar{a}\Lambda\bar{x}_{q}], and E3=𝔼⁡[x¯q⊤​Λ2​x¯q]E_{3}=\mathbb{E}[\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}\Lambda^{2}\bar{x}_{q}]. Then ℒ=12​(E1−2​E2+E3)\mathcal{L}=\frac{1}{2}(E_{1}-2E_{2}+E_{3}).

For E1E_{1}:

E1\displaystyle E_{1} =𝔼Λ,x¯q​[x¯q⊤​S^​Λ​a¯2​Λ​S^​x¯q]=𝔼Λ,x¯q​[Tr​(x¯q⊤​S^​Λ​a¯2​Λ​S^​x¯q)]=𝔼Λ,x¯q​[Tr​(S^​Λ​a¯2​Λ​S^​x¯q​x¯q⊤)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\Lambda,\bar{x}_{q}}[\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}\hat{S}\Lambda\bar{a}^{2}\Lambda\hat{S}\bar{x}_{q}]=\mathbb{E}_{\Lambda,\bar{x}_{q}}[\text{Tr}(\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}\hat{S}\Lambda\bar{a}^{2}\Lambda\hat{S}\bar{x}_{q})]=\mathbb{E}_{\Lambda,\bar{x}_{q}}[\text{Tr}(\hat{S}\Lambda\bar{a}^{2}\Lambda\hat{S}\bar{x}_{q}\bar{x}_{q}^{\top})]
=𝔼Λ​[Tr​(S^​Λ​a¯2​Λ​S^​𝔼x¯q|Λ​[x¯q​x¯q⊤])]=𝔼Λ​[Tr​(S^​Λ​a¯2​Λ​S^​S)],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\Lambda}[\text{Tr}(\hat{S}\Lambda\bar{a}^{2}\Lambda\hat{S}\mathbb{E}_{\bar{x}_{q}|\Lambda}[\bar{x}_{q}\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}])]=\mathbb{E}_{\Lambda}[\text{Tr}(\hat{S}\Lambda\bar{a}^{2}\Lambda\hat{S}S)],

since 𝔼x¯q​[x¯q​x¯q⊤]=S\mathbb{E}_{\bar{x}_{q}}[\bar{x}_{q}\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}]=S and is independent of Λ\Lambda. As trace is linear and cyclic, and matrices are diagonal,

E1\displaystyle E_{1} =Tr​(𝔼Λ​[S^​Λ​a¯2​Λ​S^]​S)=Tr​(𝔼Λ​[Λ2]​S^2​a¯2​S)=Tr​(I​𝔼​[S^2]​a¯2​S)=Tr​(𝔼⁡[S^2]​a¯2​S),\displaystyle=\text{Tr}(\mathbb{E}_{\Lambda}[\hat{S}\Lambda\bar{a}^{2}\Lambda\hat{S}]S)=\text{Tr}(\mathbb{E}_{\Lambda}[\Lambda^{2}]\hat{S}^{2}\bar{a}^{2}S)=\text{Tr}(I\mathbb{E}[\hat{S}^{2}]\bar{a}^{2}S)=\text{Tr}(\mathbb{E}[\hat{S}^{2}]\bar{a}^{2}S),

using 𝔼⁡[Λ2]=I\mathbb{E}[\Lambda^{2}]=I and commutativity. Using 𝔼⁡[S^2]=N+1N​S2+Tr⁡(S)N​S\mathbb{E}[\hat{S}^{2}]=\frac{N+1}{N}S^{2}+\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(S)}{N}S,

E1=Tr​((N+1N​S2+Tr⁡(S)N​S)​a¯2​S).E_{1}=\text{Tr}\left(\left(\frac{N+1}{N}S^{2}+\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(S)}{N}S\right)\bar{a}^{2}S\right). (A104)

For E2E_{2}:

E2\displaystyle E_{2} =𝔼Λ,x¯q​[x¯q⊤​S^​Λ​a¯​Λ​x¯q]=𝔼Λ,x¯q​[Tr​(x¯q⊤​S^​Λ​a¯​Λ​x¯q)]=𝔼Λ,x¯q​[Tr​(S^​Λ​a¯​Λ​x¯q​x¯q⊤)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\Lambda,\bar{x}_{q}}[\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}\hat{S}\Lambda\bar{a}\Lambda\bar{x}_{q}]=\mathbb{E}_{\Lambda,\bar{x}_{q}}[\text{Tr}(\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}\hat{S}\Lambda\bar{a}\Lambda\bar{x}_{q})]=\mathbb{E}_{\Lambda,\bar{x}_{q}}[\text{Tr}(\hat{S}\Lambda\bar{a}\Lambda\bar{x}_{q}\bar{x}_{q}^{\top})]
=𝔼Λ​[Tr​(S^​Λ​a¯​Λ​𝔼x¯q|Λ​[x¯q​x¯q⊤])]=𝔼Λ​[Tr​(S^​Λ​a¯​Λ​S)]=Tr​(𝔼Λ​[S^​Λ​a¯​Λ]​S)\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\Lambda}[\text{Tr}(\hat{S}\Lambda\bar{a}\Lambda\mathbb{E}_{\bar{x}_{q}|\Lambda}[\bar{x}_{q}\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}])]=\mathbb{E}_{\Lambda}[\text{Tr}(\hat{S}\Lambda\bar{a}\Lambda S)]=\text{Tr}(\mathbb{E}_{\Lambda}[\hat{S}\Lambda\bar{a}\Lambda]S)
=Tr​(𝔼Λ​[Λ2]​S^​a¯​S)=Tr​(I​𝔼​[S^]​a¯​S)=Tr​(𝔼⁡[S^]​a¯​S)=Tr​(S​a¯​S)=Tr​(a¯​S2),\displaystyle=\text{Tr}(\mathbb{E}_{\Lambda}[\Lambda^{2}]\hat{S}\bar{a}S)=\text{Tr}(I\mathbb{E}[\hat{S}]\bar{a}S)=\text{Tr}(\mathbb{E}[\hat{S}]\bar{a}S)=\text{Tr}(S\bar{a}S)=\text{Tr}(\bar{a}S^{2}),

using 𝔼⁡[Λ2]=I\mathbb{E}[\Lambda^{2}]=I and 𝔼⁡[S^]=S\mathbb{E}[\hat{S}]=S.

E2=Tr​(a¯​S2).E_{2}=\text{Tr}(\bar{a}S^{2}). (A105)

For E3E_{3}:

E3\displaystyle E_{3} =𝔼Λ,x¯q​[x¯q⊤​Λ2​x¯q]=𝔼Λ,x¯q​[Tr​(x¯q⊤​Λ2​x¯q)]=𝔼Λ,x¯q​[Tr​(Λ2​x¯q​x¯q⊤)]=Tr​(𝔼Λ,x¯q​[Λ2​x¯q​x¯q⊤])\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\Lambda,\bar{x}_{q}}[\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}\Lambda^{2}\bar{x}_{q}]=\mathbb{E}_{\Lambda,\bar{x}_{q}}[\text{Tr}(\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}\Lambda^{2}\bar{x}_{q})]=\mathbb{E}_{\Lambda,\bar{x}_{q}}[\text{Tr}(\Lambda^{2}\bar{x}_{q}\bar{x}_{q}^{\top})]=\text{Tr}(\mathbb{E}_{\Lambda,\bar{x}_{q}}[\Lambda^{2}\bar{x}_{q}\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}])
=Tr​(𝔼Λ​[Λ2]​𝔼x¯q​[x¯q​x¯q⊤])=Tr​(I⋅S)=Tr​(S).\displaystyle=\text{Tr}(\mathbb{E}_{\Lambda}[\Lambda^{2}]\mathbb{E}_{\bar{x}_{q}}[\bar{x}_{q}\bar{x}_{q}^{\top}])=\text{Tr}(I\cdot S)=\text{Tr}(S).
E3=Tr​(S).E_{3}=\text{Tr}(S). (A106)

Substituting Equations (A104), (A105), and (A106) into ℒ=12​(E1−2​E2+E3)\mathcal{L}=\frac{1}{2}(E_{1}-2E_{2}+E_{3}):

ℒ\displaystyle\mathcal{L} =12​(Tr​((N+1N​S2+Tr⁡(S)N​S)​a¯2​S)−2​Tr​(a¯​S2)+Tr​(S))\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\left(\text{Tr}\left(\left(\frac{N+1}{N}S^{2}+\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(S)}{N}S\right)\bar{a}^{2}S\right)-2\text{Tr}\left(\bar{a}S^{2}\right)+\text{Tr}(S)\right) (A107)
=12​∑α((N+1N​sα2+Tr⁡(S)N​sα)​aα2​sα−2​aα​sα2+sα)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\alpha}\left(\left(\frac{N+1}{N}s_{\alpha}^{2}+\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(S)}{N}s_{\alpha}\right)a_{\alpha}^{2}s_{\alpha}-2a_{\alpha}s_{\alpha}^{2}+s_{\alpha}\right) (A108)
=12​∑αsα​(aα2​sα​(N+1N​sα+Tr⁡(S)N)−2​aα​sα+1).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\alpha}s_{\alpha}\left(a_{\alpha}^{2}s_{\alpha}\left(\frac{N+1}{N}s_{\alpha}+\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(S)}{N}\right)-2a_{\alpha}s_{\alpha}+1\right). (A109)

Using aα∞=1N+1N​sα+Tr⁡(S)Na_{\alpha}^{\infty}=\frac{1}{\frac{N+1}{N}s_{\alpha}+\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(S)}{N}}, or 1aα∞=N+1N​sα+Tr⁡(S)N\frac{1}{a_{\alpha}^{\infty}}=\frac{N+1}{N}s_{\alpha}+\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(S)}{N}, we can rewrite the loss as:

ℒ=12​∑αsα​(sαaα∞​aα2​(t)−2​aα​(t)​sα+1).\mathcal{L}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\alpha}s_{\alpha}\left(\frac{s_{\alpha}}{a_{\alpha}^{\infty}}a_{\alpha}^{2}(t)-2a_{\alpha}(t)s_{\alpha}+1\right). (A110)

A.13.3 Loss at Infinity and Initial Loss Behavior

As t→∞t\to\infty, aα​(t)→aα∞a_{\alpha}(t)\to a_{\alpha}^{\infty}. The loss at infinite time (converged loss) is:

ℒ⁡(∞)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\infty) =12​∑αsα​(sαaα∞​(aα∞)2−2​aα∞​sα+1)=12​∑αsα​(aα∞​sα−2​aα∞​sα+1)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\alpha}s_{\alpha}\left(\frac{s_{\alpha}}{a_{\alpha}^{\infty}}(a_{\alpha}^{\infty})^{2}-2a_{\alpha}^{\infty}s_{\alpha}+1\right)=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\alpha}s_{\alpha}\left(a_{\alpha}^{\infty}s_{\alpha}-2a_{\alpha}^{\infty}s_{\alpha}+1\right) (A111)
=12​∑αsα​(1−aα∞​sα)=12​∑αsα​(1−sαN+1N​sα+Tr⁡(S)N)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\alpha}s_{\alpha}\left(1-a_{\alpha}^{\infty}s_{\alpha}\right)=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\alpha}s_{\alpha}\left(1-\frac{s_{\alpha}}{\frac{N+1}{N}s_{\alpha}+\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(S)}{N}}\right) (A112)
=12​∑αsα​(N+1N​sα+Tr⁡(S)N−sαN+1N​sα+Tr⁡(S)N)=12​∑αsα​(1N​sα+Tr⁡(S)NN+1N​sα+Tr⁡(S)N)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\alpha}s_{\alpha}\left(\frac{\frac{N+1}{N}s_{\alpha}+\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(S)}{N}-s_{\alpha}}{\frac{N+1}{N}s_{\alpha}+\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(S)}{N}}\right)=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\alpha}s_{\alpha}\left(\frac{\frac{1}{N}s_{\alpha}+\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(S)}{N}}{\frac{N+1}{N}s_{\alpha}+\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(S)}{N}}\right) (A113)
=12​∑αsα​(1N​sα+Tr⁡(S)N)N+1N​sα+Tr⁡(S)N=12​N​∑αsα​(sα+Tr⁡(S))N+1N​sα+Tr⁡(S)N=12​∑αsα​(sα+Tr⁡(S))(N+1)​sα+Tr⁡(S).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\alpha}\frac{s_{\alpha}(\frac{1}{N}s_{\alpha}+\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(S)}{N})}{\frac{N+1}{N}s_{\alpha}+\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(S)}{N}}=\frac{1}{2N}\sum_{\alpha}\frac{s_{\alpha}(s_{\alpha}+\operatorname{Tr}(S))}{\frac{N+1}{N}s_{\alpha}+\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(S)}{N}}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\alpha}\frac{s_{\alpha}(s_{\alpha}+\operatorname{Tr}(S))}{(N+1)s_{\alpha}+\operatorname{Tr}(S)}. (A114)

To understand the initial behavior of the loss, we compute the time derivative of ℒ\mathcal{L} at t=0t=0. Using chain rule and Equation (A109):

d​ℒd​t\displaystyle\frac{d\mathcal{L}}{dt} =∑α∂ℒ∂aα​d​aαd​t=∑α12​sα​(2​aα​sα​1aα∞−2​sα)​d​aαd​t=∑αsα​(sα​aαaα∞−sα)​d​aαd​t\displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha}\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial a_{\alpha}}\frac{da_{\alpha}}{dt}=\sum_{\alpha}\frac{1}{2}s_{\alpha}\left(2a_{\alpha}s_{\alpha}\frac{1}{a_{\alpha}^{\infty}}-2s_{\alpha}\right)\frac{da_{\alpha}}{dt}=\sum_{\alpha}s_{\alpha}\left(\frac{s_{\alpha}a_{\alpha}}{a_{\alpha}^{\infty}}-s_{\alpha}\right)\frac{da_{\alpha}}{dt}
=∑αsα2​(aαaα∞−1)​d​aαd​t.\displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha}s_{\alpha}^{2}\left(\frac{a_{\alpha}}{a_{\alpha}^{\infty}}-1\right)\frac{da_{\alpha}}{dt}.

Substituting d​aαd​t=2τα​aα​(1−aα​sα∞)\frac{da_{\alpha}}{dt}=\frac{2}{\tau_{\alpha}}a_{\alpha}(1-a_{\alpha}s_{\alpha}^{\infty}) from Section A.12:

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
